cards.q: Why is the posterior pituitary classified as neural tissue rather than glandular tissue?
cards.a: It is a downgrowth of the hypothalamus made of axon terminals.
options: It is a downgrowth of the hypothalamus made of axon terminals
It is an outpocketing of the roof of the developing mouth
It is a cluster of secretory epithelial cells fed by a portal system
It is a modified sympathetic ganglion with chromaffin cells
cards.explanation: The posterior pituitary forms as a downward extension of the developing brain, so it contains axon terminals of hypothalamic neurons plus supporting glia rather than gland cells. An outpocketing of the roof of the mouth describes the anterior pituitary, which is true glandular epithelium. Secretory epithelial cells fed by a portal system also describes the anterior lobe. A modified sympathetic ganglion with chromaffin cells describes the adrenal medulla.

cards.q: Where are antidiuretic hormone and oxytocin actually synthesized?
cards.a: In cell bodies of hypothalamic neurons.
options: In secretory cells of the posterior pituitary itself
In cell bodies of hypothalamic neurons
In the median eminence capillary bed
In corticotropes of the anterior pituitary
cards.explanation: Both peptides are made in neuron cell bodies of the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei, then travel down axons to be stored in the posterior lobe until release. The posterior pituitary itself contains no cells that synthesize hormone, only the nerve terminals. The median eminence is where hypothalamic releasing hormones enter the portal blood for the anterior lobe. Corticotropes make ACTH, an anterior pituitary product.

cards.q: What is the main target of antidiuretic hormone?
cards.a: The collecting duct of the kidney.
options: The glomerular capillary wall
The loop of Henle thin descending limb
The collecting duct of the kidney
The wall of the urinary bladder
cards.explanation: ADH binds receptors on collecting duct principal cells, which is where the final adjustment of water reabsorption is made. The glomerular capillary wall filters plasma and is not hormone gated for water. The thin descending limb is already freely permeable to water without hormonal control. The bladder stores urine and does not change its composition.

cards.q: How does antidiuretic hormone increase water reabsorption?
cards.a: It inserts aquaporin water channels into the apical membrane.
options: It opens sodium channels that drag water along with them
It pumps water directly across the wall of the tubule
It increases the filtration rate at the glomerulus instead
It inserts aquaporin water channels into the apical membrane
cards.explanation: ADH triggers the insertion of stored aquaporin-2 channels into the apical membrane, so water can follow the medullary osmotic gradient out of the tubule. Sodium channels move Na+, and although water follows solute, that is not the hormone specific step ADH controls here. ADH does not act on filtration rate. No pump moves water directly, since water always moves down its own osmotic gradient.

cards.q: What is the strongest ordinary stimulus for antidiuretic hormone release?
cards.a: A rise in plasma osmolarity.
options: A rise in plasma osmolarity
A fall in plasma potassium
A rise in plasma calcium
A fall in plasma glucose
cards.explanation: Hypothalamic osmoreceptors fire when plasma osmolarity climbs even a percent or two, and that is the most sensitive trigger for ADH release. Plasma potassium is a stimulus for aldosterone, not ADH. Plasma calcium is monitored by the parathyroid glands. Plasma glucose drives insulin and glucagon secretion from the islets.

cards.q: Which two tissues does oxytocin act on in a nursing mother?
cards.a: Uterine smooth muscle and breast myoepithelial cells.
options: Kidney collecting duct and uterine smooth muscle
Uterine smooth muscle and breast myoepithelial cells
Breast alveolar secretory cells and liver
Ovarian follicle cells and uterine endometrium
cards.explanation: Oxytocin contracts uterine smooth muscle during labor and squeezes the myoepithelial cells wrapped around the milk alveoli, which is what ejects milk already made. The collecting duct is the ADH target, not the oxytocin target. Alveolar secretory cells make milk under prolactin, but they do not contract. Ovarian follicle cells respond to FSH and LH from the anterior lobe.

cards.q: What stimulus triggers oxytocin release during breastfeeding?
cards.a: Suckling at the nipple.
options: A rise in plasma prolactin
Stretch of the milk ducts by stored milk
Suckling at the nipple
A fall in plasma estrogen after delivery
cards.explanation: Mechanoreceptors in the nipple fire during suckling and send that signal to the hypothalamic neurons that release oxytocin, which is a neuroendocrine reflex. Prolactin drives milk synthesis but does not itself trigger oxytocin. Duct stretch does not cause release, and in fact unremoved milk suppresses further production. Falling estrogen permits lactation to begin but is not the moment to moment trigger.

cards.q: What is the other name for antidiuretic hormone?
cards.a: Vasopressin.
options: Angiotensin II
Aldosterone
Atrial natriuretic peptide
Vasopressin
cards.explanation: ADH is called vasopressin because at high concentrations it also constricts arterioles and raises blood pressure. Aldosterone is an adrenal steroid that conserves sodium rather than water alone. Atrial natriuretic peptide does the opposite, promoting salt and water loss. Angiotensin II is a vasoconstrictor but it is generated in plasma, not released from the pituitary.

cards.q: A student drinks two liters of water quickly. What happens to antidiuretic hormone release?
cards.a: It falls, because plasma osmolarity drops.
options: It falls, because plasma osmolarity drops
It rises, because plasma volume increased
It rises, because the kidney must handle more water
It is unchanged, since only sodium intake affects it
cards.explanation: Diluting the plasma lowers osmolarity, the osmoreceptors quiet down, ADH release falls, and the collecting duct removes aquaporins so a large dilute urine is passed. Increased volume does not raise ADH, it lowers it through the low pressure stretch receptors. The kidney handles the extra water by making less ADH, not more. Water alone changes osmolarity, so sodium intake is not the only input.

cards.q: A hiker has gone eight hours without water on a hot day. What is her urine like?
cards.a: Small in volume and concentrated.
options: Large in volume and dilute
Small in volume and concentrated
Large in volume and concentrated
Small in volume and dilute
cards.explanation: Water loss raises plasma osmolarity, ADH rises, aquaporins go into the collecting duct, and water is reclaimed so the urine is scant and concentrated. Large and dilute is the water loaded response, when ADH is low. Large and concentrated happens only when a solute such as glucose forces an osmotic diuresis. Small and dilute is not physiologically possible as a normal response, since low volume comes from reclaiming water.

cards.q: Alcohol suppresses antidiuretic hormone secretion. What does that predict about urine output?
cards.a: Urine volume rises above the volume of fluid drunk.
options: Urine volume falls and osmolarity rises
Urine volume is unchanged but sodium loss rises
Urine volume rises above the volume of fluid drunk
Urine volume falls because plasma volume falls first
cards.explanation: With ADH suppressed the collecting duct stays water impermeable, so water that would normally be reclaimed is lost and the person can excrete more fluid than they drank, which is why alcohol dehydrates. Falling volume with rising osmolarity is the high ADH pattern. ADH controls water rather than sodium handling, so a pure sodium loss is not the prediction. Plasma volume falls as a consequence here, not as the cause.

cards.q: A patient loses posterior pituitary function after surgery. What pattern of urine do you predict?
cards.a: Very large volumes of dilute urine.
options: Very small volumes of concentrated urine
Very large volumes of concentrated urine
Normal volume with glucose present
Very large volumes of dilute urine
cards.explanation: Without ADH the collecting duct cannot insert aquaporins, so water passes straight through and the person makes many liters of dilute urine each day, the picture called diabetes insipidus. Small concentrated volumes require ADH to be present and working. Glucose in the urine points to diabetes mellitus, a different problem entirely. Large volumes of concentrated urine would require a filtered solute load, which is not the case here.

cards.q: During nursing, suckling causes oxytocin release, which causes milk ejection, which encourages more suckling. What kind of control is this?
cards.a: Positive feedback.
options: Positive feedback
Negative feedback
Feedforward control
Tonic inhibition
cards.explanation: The response amplifies the original stimulus rather than shutting it off, which is the defining feature of positive feedback, and the loop ends when the infant stops feeding. Negative feedback would mean milk ejection reduces oxytocin release. Feedforward means anticipating a change before it happens, such as insulin rising at the sight of food. Tonic inhibition describes a steady brake, not an amplifying loop.

cards.q: Plasma osmolarity rises from 290 to 300 mOsm/L. What happens at the collecting duct?
cards.a: More aquaporins are inserted and more water is reabsorbed.
options: Aquaporins are withdrawn and far more water is excreted instead
More aquaporins are inserted and more water is reabsorbed
Sodium pumps are inhibited and more sodium is excreted
Filtration rate rises so much more urine is formed
cards.explanation: A ten milliosmole rise is a large osmotic signal, so ADH release climbs sharply and drives aquaporin-2 insertion, reclaiming water to bring osmolarity back down. Withdrawing aquaporins is what happens when osmolarity falls. Sodium handling in this segment is aldosterone territory, not the osmoreceptor pathway. Filtration rate is regulated at the glomerulus and is not the target of this reflex.

cards.q: A trauma patient has lost a liter of blood. Besides osmolarity, what else drives antidiuretic hormone release here?
cards.a: Reduced firing from arterial and atrial stretch receptors.
options: Reduced plasma potassium sensed by the adrenal cortex
Increased firing from hypothalamic thermoreceptors
Reduced firing from arterial and atrial stretch receptors
Increased carbon dioxide sensed by central chemoreceptors
cards.explanation: A large volume loss unloads baroreceptors and atrial stretch receptors, and their reduced firing releases the brake on ADH, so ADH rises to conserve water and support pressure. Thermoreceptors drive sweating and skin blood flow, not ADH. Potassium sensing by the adrenal cortex governs aldosterone. Central chemoreceptors adjust ventilation rather than pituitary output.

cards.q: A patient after a head injury makes 9 L of dilute urine per day. Plasma sodium is high and plasma osmolarity is 310 mOsm/L. What is the most likely explanation?
cards.a: Antidiuretic hormone release has failed, so water is not reclaimed.
options: Antidiuretic hormone is being released in great excess
Filtered glucose has exceeded the tubular transport maximum here
Aldosterone is being released in excess, wasting both salt and water
Antidiuretic hormone release has failed, so water is not reclaimed
cards.explanation: High plasma osmolarity should be a maximal ADH stimulus, so a dilute high volume urine in the face of that stimulus means the ADH signal itself is missing, which fits injury to the hypothalamus or posterior lobe. Excess ADH would give concentrated urine and low plasma sodium. Excess aldosterone retains sodium and does not produce dilute high volume urine. Filtered glucose above the transport maximum would give large volumes but the urine would carry glucose and osmolarity would not be dilute.

cards.q: A patient secretes antidiuretic hormone continuously regardless of plasma osmolarity. Predict plasma sodium and urine osmolarity.
cards.a: Plasma sodium falls and urine osmolarity is high.
options: Plasma sodium falls and urine osmolarity is high
Plasma sodium rises and urine osmolarity is high
Plasma sodium falls and urine osmolarity is low
Plasma sodium rises and urine osmolarity is low
cards.explanation: Unregulated ADH keeps aquaporins in place, so water is retained and dilutes the plasma, dropping sodium, while the small urine that is passed is concentrated. Rising sodium with concentrated urine would mean water is being lost, not retained. Falling sodium with dilute urine is the pattern of drinking far too much water with ADH properly suppressed. Rising sodium with dilute urine is the picture of absent ADH.

cards.q: The pituitary stalk is cut, separating the hypothalamus from both pituitary lobes. Why does antidiuretic hormone secretion stop even though the neurons that make it are intact?
cards.a: The axons that carry the hormone to its release site are severed.
options: The releasing hormone can no longer reach the portal blood
The axons that carry the hormone to its release site are severed
The hypothalamic neurons lose their osmoreceptor input
The posterior lobe cells can no longer synthesize the peptide
cards.explanation: ADH reaches the circulation only by traveling down hypothalamic axons to terminals in the posterior lobe, so cutting the stalk cuts the delivery route even though the cell bodies survive. Portal blood delivery of releasing hormones is how the anterior lobe is controlled, a separate pathway. Osmoreceptors sit in the hypothalamus itself and are not disconnected by a stalk cut. The posterior lobe never synthesized the peptide, so losing synthesis there cannot be the reason.

cards.q: A woman is severely dehydrated and also nursing. Both hormones of the posterior pituitary are elevated. Which pairing of effects do you predict?
cards.a: Water reabsorption rises in the kidney and milk is ejected from the breast.
options: Water reabsorption rises in the kidney and milk synthesis increases
Sodium reabsorption rises in the kidney and milk synthesis increases
Water reabsorption rises in the kidney and milk is ejected from the breast
Sodium reabsorption rises in the kidney and milk is ejected from the breast
cards.explanation: ADH acts on the collecting duct to reclaim water, and oxytocin contracts myoepithelial cells to eject milk that has already been made, so those two effects appear together. Sodium reabsorption is the job of aldosterone, not either posterior pituitary hormone. Milk synthesis is driven by prolactin from the anterior lobe, so it is not part of the oxytocin response. Water reabsorption paired with milk ejection is the only combination that matches the actual targets of these two hormones.

cards.q: Which structure secretes growth hormone?
cards.a: The anterior pituitary.
options: The hypothalamus
The anterior pituitary
The posterior pituitary
The liver
cards.explanation: Somatotropes in the anterior pituitary make and release growth hormone into the general circulation. The hypothalamus supplies the releasing and inhibiting signals but does not make growth hormone itself. The posterior pituitary stores only ADH and oxytocin. The liver responds to growth hormone by making IGF-1, so it is a target rather than the source.

cards.q: Which organ produces most of the circulating insulin like growth factor 1?
cards.a: The liver.
options: The kidney
The anterior pituitary
The liver
The epiphyseal plate
cards.explanation: Growth hormone binds hepatocytes and the liver releases IGF-1 into the blood, which is how most of the growth promoting effect is actually delivered. The kidney makes erythropoietin and activates vitamin D, not IGF-1. The anterior pituitary makes growth hormone itself, one step earlier in the chain. The epiphyseal plate is the tissue IGF-1 acts on, and its local production is small compared with hepatic output.

cards.q: What is the direct effect of growth hormone on adipose tissue?
cards.a: It increases lipolysis and releases fatty acids.
options: It blocks fatty acid entry into mitochondria
It increases triglyceride storage in fat cells
It converts fatty acids into glucose
It increases lipolysis and releases fatty acids
cards.explanation: Growth hormone acts directly on fat cells to break down stored triglyceride, freeing fatty acids as an alternative fuel so glucose is spared for other tissues. Increasing storage is the effect of insulin, which is the opposing signal. Fatty acids cannot be converted into glucose in humans, so that option is not a real pathway. Blocking mitochondrial entry of fatty acids would prevent their use, the opposite of what growth hormone accomplishes.

cards.q: What is the direct effect of growth hormone on plasma glucose?
cards.a: It raises plasma glucose.
options: It raises plasma glucose
It lowers plasma glucose
It leaves plasma glucose unchanged
It lowers plasma glucose only during exercise
cards.explanation: Growth hormone opposes insulin in muscle and fat, reducing glucose uptake while the liver adds glucose to the blood, which is why it is described as having a diabetogenic action. Lowering glucose is the job of insulin. Glucose does not stay unchanged, since the anti insulin effect is measurable within hours. Exercise does not reverse the direction of the effect.

cards.q: Which growth hormone action is carried out mainly through insulin like growth factor 1?
cards.a: Lengthening of long bones at the epiphyseal plate.
options: Release of fatty acids from stored adipose tissue
Lengthening of long bones at the epiphyseal plate
Reduction of glucose uptake by skeletal muscle
Increased hepatic output of glucose to the blood
cards.explanation: IGF-1 is the mediator that drives cartilage cell division and matrix production at the growth plate, along with general protein synthesis, so linear growth is the classic indirect action. Lipolysis, reduced glucose uptake, and hepatic glucose output are the direct metabolic actions of growth hormone on its own receptors. Splitting the actions this way is the point of the distinction between direct and mediated effects.

cards.q: Which hypothalamic hormone inhibits growth hormone release?
cards.a: Somatostatin.
options: Growth hormone releasing hormone
Corticotropin releasing hormone
Somatostatin
Thyrotropin releasing hormone
cards.explanation: Somatostatin from the hypothalamus is the brake on somatotropes, and growth hormone output reflects the balance between it and the releasing hormone. Growth hormone releasing hormone is the accelerator, not the brake. Corticotropin releasing hormone drives ACTH and the cortisol axis. Thyrotropin releasing hormone drives TSH and the thyroid axis.

cards.q: Excess growth hormone in a child whose epiphyseal plates are still open produces which condition?
cards.a: Gigantism.
options: Cretinism
Acromegaly
Pituitary dwarfism
Gigantism
cards.explanation: Open plates can still add length, so excess growth hormone before closure produces an unusually tall person with roughly normal proportions. Acromegaly is the same hormone excess after the plates have closed. Pituitary dwarfism is growth hormone deficiency in childhood. Cretinism results from untreated thyroid hormone deficiency in infancy, a different hormone entirely.

cards.q: Excess growth hormone in an adult whose epiphyseal plates have closed produces which condition?
cards.a: Acromegaly.
options: Acromegaly
Pituitary dwarfism
Gigantism
Myxedema
cards.explanation: With the plates closed no further length is possible, so bone grows by thickening and the hands, feet, and jaw enlarge, which is acromegaly. Gigantism requires open plates and therefore childhood onset. Pituitary dwarfism is the deficiency state, not the excess. Myxedema is severe adult hypothyroidism and has nothing to do with growth hormone.

cards.q: A child produces almost no growth hormone from infancy. What do you predict about his adult stature and body proportions?
cards.a: Short with roughly normal proportions.
options: Short with a normal trunk and very short limbs
Short with roughly normal proportions
Tall with unusually long limbs
Normal height with enlarged hands and jaw
cards.explanation: Growth hormone deficiency slows growth at every plate at once, so the child ends up small but proportioned, the picture of pituitary dwarfism. Short limbs with a normal trunk is the pattern of a cartilage disorder such as achondroplasia, not a hormone deficiency. Tall with long limbs points to excess growth hormone or delayed plate closure. Normal height with enlarged hands and jaw is acromegaly, an adult onset excess.

cards.q: A 45 year old finds that his ring size and shoe size have both increased over three years and his jaw has become more prominent. Which hormone problem does this fit?
cards.a: Growth hormone excess after epiphyseal closure.
options: Growth hormone deficiency in adulthood
Growth hormone excess before epiphyseal closure
Growth hormone excess after epiphyseal closure
Insulin like growth factor 1 deficiency
cards.explanation: After the plates close, extra growth hormone can only thicken bone and expand soft tissue, so hands, feet, and facial bones enlarge without any gain in height. Deficiency in adulthood reduces lean mass and bone density rather than enlarging the extremities. Excess before closure would have made him unusually tall as well. IGF-1 deficiency would blunt growth, not exaggerate it.

cards.q: A person with a defective growth hormone receptor has high plasma growth hormone but very low IGF-1. What do you predict about growth?
cards.a: Growth is poor, because the mediator is missing.
options: Growth is excessive, because growth hormone is high
Growth is normal until the plates close, then slows
Growth is normal, because growth hormone acts directly on bone
Growth is poor, because the mediator is missing
cards.explanation: Linear growth depends on IGF-1, so a broken receptor upstream means the liver never releases the mediator and the child grows poorly no matter how high the growth hormone level climbs. High growth hormone cannot drive growth if the signal cannot be received. Growth hormone does not lengthen bone by acting directly on the plate to any meaningful degree. Growth failure is present from early childhood, not delayed until closure.

cards.q: What happens to growth hormone secretion during a prolonged fast, and why does that make metabolic sense?
cards.a: It rises, mobilizing fat and sparing glucose.
options: It rises, mobilizing fat and sparing glucose
It falls, reducing the demand for fuel
It falls, allowing insulin to store the remaining glucose
It rises, increasing glucose uptake into muscle
cards.explanation: Fasting increases growth hormone secretion, which frees fatty acids for muscle and other tissues while limiting glucose uptake so the brain keeps its supply. A fall would remove that fuel switching signal at the moment it is most needed. Insulin secretion falls during a fast, so there is little glucose storage to permit. Growth hormone reduces rather than increases glucose uptake into muscle.

cards.q: An adult with closed epiphyseal plates is given growth hormone. What effect on height do you predict?
cards.a: No increase in height, since no plate cartilage remains.
options: A gain of several centimeters of height over a year
No increase in height, since no plate cartilage remains
A gain in height only if plasma IGF-1 also rises
A loss of height from increased bone resorption
cards.explanation: Lengthening requires proliferating cartilage at the epiphyseal plate, and once that plate has been replaced by bone the substrate for length is simply gone. A gain of centimeters is impossible for the same reason. Raising IGF-1 does not help, because IGF-1 needs plate cartilage to act on. Growth hormone does not cause height loss, since it favors bone formation rather than resorption.

cards.q: A patient with a growth hormone secreting tumor is found to have a fasting plasma glucose of 130 mg/dL. Which growth hormone action explains this?
cards.a: Its direct anti insulin action in muscle and fat.
options: Its IGF-1 mediated action on cartilage
Its stimulation of insulin secretion by beta cells
Its direct anti insulin action in muscle and fat
Its inhibition of hepatic glucose output
cards.explanation: Growth hormone directly opposes insulin, cutting glucose uptake into muscle and fat while the liver keeps releasing glucose, so fasting glucose drifts upward. The IGF-1 mediated action is on growth, not on glucose handling. Beta cells actually work harder to compensate here, but that is a response to the high glucose rather than the cause. Growth hormone raises hepatic glucose output rather than inhibiting it.

cards.q: A child grows poorly. Growth hormone is normal or high, IGF-1 is very low, and liver function is severely impaired. What best explains the growth failure?
cards.a: The damaged liver cannot generate IGF-1 in response to the hormone.
options: The pituitary is not secreting enough growth hormone at all
The epiphyseal plates have already closed prematurely
Somatostatin is suppressing the epiphyseal plates directly in the bone
The damaged liver cannot generate IGF-1 in response to the hormone
cards.explanation: Growth hormone works on bone through hepatic IGF-1, so liver failure breaks the chain at the mediator step and growth stalls even with plenty of hormone upstream. Inadequate pituitary secretion is ruled out by the normal or high growth hormone level. Somatostatin acts on the pituitary to reduce growth hormone release and does not act on plates. Premature plate closure would show as an advanced bone age with the plates gone, not as a low IGF-1.

cards.q: A patient with acromegaly is treated with a drug that mimics somatostatin. Trace the expected changes in growth hormone, IGF-1, and soft tissue swelling.
cards.a: Growth hormone falls, IGF-1 falls, and soft tissue swelling decreases.
options: Growth hormone falls, IGF-1 falls, and soft tissue swelling decreases
Growth hormone rises, IGF-1 falls, and soft tissue swelling decreases
Growth hormone falls, IGF-1 rises, and soft tissue swelling decreases
Growth hormone falls, IGF-1 is unchanged, and soft tissue swelling increases
cards.explanation: Somatostatin inhibits the somatotropes, so growth hormone drops, hepatic IGF-1 drops with it because it is downstream, and the soft tissue enlargement driven by both hormones recedes. IGF-1 cannot rise while its driver is falling. Growth hormone cannot rise under a somatostatin like drug, which is inhibitory. Unchanged IGF-1 with worsening swelling would mean the drug had no effect at all.

cards.q: Two people have the same growth hormone secreting tumor. One developed it at age 10 and one at age 40. How will their presentations differ?
cards.a: The child becomes very tall as well as thick boned, the adult only thick boned.
options: The adult becomes very tall, and the child only becomes thick boned instead
The child becomes very tall as well as thick boned, the adult only thick boned
Both become very tall, but only the adult has a high plasma glucose level
Both become thick boned, and neither of them gains any height at all
cards.explanation: Open epiphyseal plates at age 10 allow length to be added, so the child grows tall and also thickens, while the adult with closed plates can only thicken. The adult cannot gain height because the plate cartilage is gone. The anti insulin effect on glucose occurs at either age, so it does not separate them. Saying neither gains height ignores the open plates in the ten year old.

cards.q: A patient with growth hormone excess has elevated glucose and elevated insulin at the same time. What does that combination tell you?
cards.a: The tissues are resisting insulin, so beta cells are compensating.
options: The beta cells have been destroyed, so glucose cannot be cleared
Insulin is being secreted normally and the glucose reading is an error
The tissues are resisting insulin, so beta cells are compensating
Growth hormone is directly stimulating hepatic glycogen storage
cards.explanation: High insulin alongside high glucose means insulin is present but not working well, which is exactly the anti insulin state growth hormone creates in muscle and fat, and the beta cells raise output to keep up. Destroyed beta cells would give high glucose with low insulin. Two abnormal values that fit a known mechanism are not an error. Growth hormone opposes storage and raises hepatic glucose release rather than promoting glycogen storage.

cards.q: Which element must be trapped by the thyroid gland to build thyroid hormone?
cards.a: Iodine.
options: Iron
Zinc
Iodine
Selenium
cards.explanation: Thyroid follicular cells actively pump iodide from the blood and attach it to tyrosine residues, so iodine is built into the hormone molecule itself. Iron is required for hemoglobin and for cytochromes, not for thyroid hormone synthesis. Zinc is a cofactor for many enzymes but is not incorporated into T3 or T4. Selenium is needed by the deiodinase enzymes that convert T4 to T3, a later step, but it is not part of the hormone.

cards.q: Which protein stores thyroid hormone in the follicular colloid?
cards.a: Thyroglobulin.
options: Transthyretin
Thyroid binding globulin
Thyroid peroxidase
Thyroglobulin
cards.explanation: Thyroglobulin is the large protein in the colloid whose tyrosine residues are iodinated and coupled, so the gland stores months of hormone inside it. Thyroid binding globulin is the plasma carrier that transports hormone in the blood, outside the gland. Thyroid peroxidase is the enzyme that does the iodinating, not the storage scaffold. Transthyretin is another plasma transport protein.

cards.q: What does thyroid peroxidase do during hormone synthesis?
cards.a: It oxidizes iodide and attaches it to tyrosine residues.
options: It oxidizes iodide and attaches it to tyrosine residues
It transports iodide into the follicular cell
It removes an iodine atom to convert T4 into T3
It splits hormone free from thyroglobulin in the cell
cards.explanation: Thyroid peroxidase oxidizes trapped iodide and adds it to tyrosines on thyroglobulin, then couples the iodinated tyrosines to form T3 and T4, which is why blocking it stops synthesis. Iodide transport into the cell is the job of the sodium iodide symporter. Removing an iodine from T4 is done by deiodinase enzymes in peripheral tissues. Lysosomal enzymes free the hormone from thyroglobulin after the colloid is taken back into the cell.

cards.q: Which thyroid hormone is the more potent form at the target cell?
options: T4, because it is secreted in greater amounts
T3
Both are equally potent
Neither is active until bound to thyroglobulin
cards.explanation: T3 binds the nuclear thyroid receptor with much higher affinity, so it is the form that actually drives gene transcription in the target cell. T4 is indeed secreted in far greater amounts, but it functions largely as a circulating reservoir that is converted to T3. Equal potency would make the conversion step pointless. Binding to thyroglobulin is a storage arrangement inside the gland, not an activation step in the target tissue.

cards.q: What do deiodinase enzymes in peripheral tissues do to T4?
cards.a: They remove one iodine to make T3.
options: They add one iodine to make T3
They bind T4 to a plasma carrier protein
They remove one iodine to make T3
They break the hormone down into free tyrosine
cards.explanation: Peripheral deiodinases strip a single iodine from T4 to yield the more active T3, which lets each tissue tune how much active hormone it gets. Adding iodine is backwards, since T4 already carries four iodine atoms and T3 carries three. Binding to a carrier protein happens in plasma and is not an enzymatic conversion. Complete breakdown to tyrosine is degradation, not activation.

cards.q: Which anterior pituitary hormone stimulates the thyroid gland?
cards.a: Thyroid stimulating hormone.
options: Thyrotropin releasing hormone
Growth hormone
Adrenocorticotropic hormone
Thyroid stimulating hormone
cards.explanation: TSH from the anterior pituitary drives iodide trapping, hormone synthesis, and release, and it also makes the gland grow when it is chronically elevated. Thyrotropin releasing hormone comes from the hypothalamus and acts on the pituitary, one step earlier. ACTH drives the adrenal cortex. Growth hormone acts mainly through hepatic IGF-1 and does not stimulate the thyroid.

cards.q: What is the effect of thyroid hormone on basal metabolic rate?
cards.a: It increases basal metabolic rate.
options: It increases basal metabolic rate
It decreases basal metabolic rate
It has no effect on basal metabolic rate
It increases it only in skeletal muscle
cards.explanation: Thyroid hormone increases the number of mitochondria and the activity of metabolic enzymes in nearly every tissue, so oxygen consumption and heat production rise. A decrease is what happens when the hormone is deficient. No effect would leave most of the signs of thyroid disease unexplained. The effect is body wide, not confined to skeletal muscle.

cards.q: Which thyroid cell type secretes T3 and T4?
cards.a: Follicular cells.
options: Parafollicular C cells
Follicular cells
Chief cells
Chromaffin cells
cards.explanation: Follicular cells form the ring around the colloid, trap iodide, and secrete T3 and T4. Parafollicular C cells sit between the follicles and secrete calcitonin instead. Chief cells belong to the parathyroid glands and secrete parathyroid hormone. Chromaffin cells belong to the adrenal medulla and secrete catecholamines.

cards.q: A patient reports heat intolerance, a resting heart rate of 105, weight loss despite a good appetite, and tremor. What underlying rate of metabolism does this fit?
cards.a: An increased metabolic rate from excess thyroid hormone.
options: A normal metabolic rate with excess cortisol
A decreased metabolic rate from thyroid hormone deficiency
An increased metabolic rate from excess thyroid hormone
A decreased metabolic rate from iodine excess
cards.explanation: Every one of these signs follows from burning fuel faster, since extra heat must be shed, the heart is driven harder, and intake cannot keep up with expenditure. Deficiency produces the mirror image, with cold intolerance and weight gain. Excess cortisol tends to add central weight rather than cause loss. Iodine excess does not by itself lower metabolic rate in this pattern.

cards.q: A patient reports feeling cold when others are comfortable, gaining weight on an unchanged diet, constipation, and a heart rate of 52. Which state does this describe?
cards.a: Hypothyroidism, with a reduced metabolic rate.
options: Hyperthyroidism, with a raised metabolic rate
Hyperthyroidism, with a reduced metabolic rate
Normal thyroid function with iron deficiency
Hypothyroidism, with a reduced metabolic rate
cards.explanation: Slower metabolism means less heat produced, fewer calories burned, slower gut motility, and less stimulation of the heart, which is exactly this cluster. Hyperthyroidism gives the opposite picture in every one of those systems. Iron deficiency causes fatigue but not cold intolerance with slow bowels and bradycardia. Hyperthyroidism with a reduced metabolic rate is self contradictory.

cards.q: A person's diet has contained almost no iodine for a year. Predict plasma T4, plasma TSH, and gland size.
cards.a: T4 low, TSH high, gland enlarged.
options: T4 low, TSH high, gland enlarged
T4 low, TSH low, gland shrunken
T4 high, TSH low, gland enlarged
T4 normal, TSH normal, gland enlarged
cards.explanation: Without iodine the gland cannot make hormone, T4 falls, negative feedback is lost so TSH climbs, and sustained TSH stimulation makes the gland grow into a goiter. Low TSH with low T4 would point to a pituitary problem rather than a substrate shortage. High T4 is impossible without iodine. Normal values would not explain why the gland enlarged.

cards.q: Thyroid hormone increases the number of beta adrenergic receptors on cardiac muscle. What does this predict about the heart in hyperthyroidism?
cards.a: The heart responds more strongly to a given level of catecholamines.
options: The heart becomes largely insensitive to the catecholamines
The heart responds more strongly to a given level of catecholamines
Catecholamine secretion from the adrenal medulla falls sharply
The heart rate is set entirely by the thyroid hormone itself
cards.explanation: More receptors means the same plasma epinephrine and norepinephrine produce a larger effect, which is the permissive action that explains the tachycardia and tremor of hyperthyroidism. Insensitivity would follow from receptor loss, which is the hypothyroid direction. Adrenal medullary output is not reduced by thyroid hormone. Thyroid hormone amplifies the sympathetic signal rather than replacing it.

cards.q: A drug blocks thyroid peroxidase. Predict the effect on plasma T4 over the next several weeks.
cards.a: T4 falls gradually as stored hormone is used up.
options: T4 falls immediately within an hour
T4 rises because stored colloid is released
T4 falls gradually as stored hormone is used up
T4 is unaffected because peripheral conversion continues
cards.explanation: Blocking peroxidase stops new synthesis, but the colloid holds weeks of ready made hormone, so the plasma level declines slowly as that reserve is released and cleared. An immediate fall would only happen if release rather than synthesis were blocked. Colloid release does not increase in response to the block. Peripheral conversion changes T4 into T3 and cannot create new hormone.

cards.q: An infant with untreated thyroid hormone deficiency from birth develops which lasting problem?
cards.a: Impaired nervous system development and stunted growth.
options: Early puberty with unusually rapid bone maturation
Excessive linear growth with entirely normal intellect
Enlarged hands and jaw with normal adult height
Impaired nervous system development and stunted growth
cards.explanation: Thyroid hormone is required for normal brain development and for skeletal growth in the first years, so untreated deficiency causes both cognitive impairment and short stature, the condition called cretinism. Excessive linear growth is the opposite of what deficiency does. Enlarged hands and jaw with normal height is acromegaly, a growth hormone problem. Deficiency delays rather than accelerates bone maturation and puberty.

cards.q: In a patient whose thyroid gland itself is overactive, what happens to TSH?
cards.a: TSH falls, because high thyroid hormone suppresses the pituitary.
options: TSH falls, because high thyroid hormone suppresses the pituitary
TSH rises, because the gland is working harder
TSH stays normal, because the thyroid is not pituitary controlled
TSH rises first and then falls once the gland enlarges
cards.explanation: Thyroid hormone feeds back negatively on the hypothalamus and anterior pituitary, so when the gland overproduces on its own, TSH is driven down to a very low level. Rising TSH would be the cause of overactivity, not the response to it. The thyroid is under pituitary control, which is why the feedback works. There is no phase of high TSH in a gland that is autonomously overproducing.

cards.q: A patient has low plasma T4 and high plasma TSH. Where is the problem?
cards.a: In the thyroid gland itself.
options: In the hypothalamus
In the thyroid gland itself
In the anterior pituitary
In the peripheral deiodinase enzymes
cards.explanation: A high TSH shows the pituitary is sensing low hormone and pushing hard, so the failure to respond must lie in the gland, which is what primary hypothyroidism means. A hypothalamic problem would lower TSH along with T4. A pituitary problem would also give a low TSH, since it could not produce the drive. A deiodinase problem would reduce T3 while leaving T4 normal or high.

cards.q: A different patient has low plasma T4 and low plasma TSH. What does this pattern indicate?
cards.a: The pituitary is not producing enough TSH to drive the gland.
options: The thyroid gland has been destroyed by autoantibodies
Dietary iodine has been severely deficient in this patient
The pituitary is not producing enough TSH to drive the gland
Excess thyroid hormone is being taken by mouth daily
cards.explanation: When hormone is low, TSH should be high, so a low TSH means the drive itself has failed and the problem sits above the gland in the pituitary or hypothalamus. Destruction of the gland or iodine deficiency would both leave the pituitary intact and TSH would be high. Excess hormone taken by mouth would suppress TSH but plasma T4 would be high, not low.

cards.q: Thyroid hormone increases the number and activity of Na+/K+ ATPase pumps throughout the body. Trace how that raises body temperature.
cards.a: More ATP is hydrolyzed by the pumps, and that energy leaves as heat.
options: The pumps generate heat by moving ions against friction in the membrane
The pumps raise plasma sodium, which raises the hypothalamic set point
The pumps constrict skin arterioles and trap heat in the core
More ATP is hydrolyzed by the pumps, and that energy leaves as heat
cards.explanation: Running more pumps consumes more ATP, cells burn more fuel and use more oxygen to replace it, and much of the energy released in that cycle appears as heat. Ion movement through a channel does not generate meaningful frictional heat. Skin arteriole tone is a vascular response controlled by the sympathetic nervous system, not by the pumps. Plasma sodium is held nearly constant and the hypothalamic set point is not raised by thyroid hormone.

cards.q: A person has been taking too much thyroid hormone for months. Predict oxygen consumption, appetite, and body weight together.
cards.a: Oxygen consumption up, appetite up, weight down.
options: Oxygen consumption up, appetite up, weight down
Oxygen consumption up, appetite down, weight down
Oxygen consumption down, appetite up, weight up
Oxygen consumption up, appetite up, weight up
cards.explanation: A raised metabolic rate burns more oxygen and more fuel, hunger rises in response, but intake usually fails to keep pace with expenditure so weight still falls. Appetite going down does not fit a high metabolic demand. Falling oxygen consumption is the hypothyroid pattern. Weight gain would require intake to exceed the increased expenditure, which is not the usual outcome.

cards.q: Which hormone is secreted by the zona glomerulosa?
cards.a: Aldosterone.
options: Cortisol
Epinephrine
Dehydroepiandrosterone
Aldosterone
cards.explanation: The outermost cortical zone, the glomerulosa, is the only tissue with the enzyme needed to finish aldosterone, so it is the sole source of that hormone. Cortisol comes from the middle zone, the fasciculata. Dehydroepiandrosterone comes from the innermost cortical zone, the reticularis. Epinephrine comes from the adrenal medulla, which is not cortex at all.

cards.q: Which hormone is secreted by the zona fasciculata?
cards.a: Cortisol.
options: Cortisol
Norepinephrine
Aldosterone
Androstenedione
cards.explanation: The broad middle zone, the fasciculata, is the main source of cortisol and it is the zone that grows under ACTH stimulation. Aldosterone is made in the outer glomerulosa. Norepinephrine is a medullary catecholamine, not a cortical steroid. Androstenedione is an adrenal androgen from the inner reticularis.

cards.q: Which hormones are secreted by the zona reticularis?
cards.a: The adrenal androgens.
options: The mineralocorticoids
The adrenal androgens
The catecholamines
The glucocorticoids only
cards.explanation: The innermost cortical zone, the reticularis, secretes weak androgens such as dehydroepiandrosterone that are converted to stronger androgens in peripheral tissue. Mineralocorticoids means aldosterone, which is a glomerulosa product. Catecholamines come from the medulla. Glucocorticoid production belongs mainly to the fasciculata, although the reticularis contributes some.

cards.q: What is the primary action of aldosterone?
cards.a: It increases sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion in the distal nephron.
options: It increases water reabsorption in the collecting duct by adding aquaporins
It increases plasma glucose by driving hepatic gluconeogenesis in the liver
It increases sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion in the distal nephron
It increases calcium reabsorption in the distal tubule of the nephron
cards.explanation: Aldosterone acts on principal cells of the distal tubule and collecting duct to add sodium channels and pumps, so sodium is retained and potassium is lost into the urine. Direct control of water permeability is the job of ADH, although water does follow the retained sodium. Driving gluconeogenesis is a cortisol action. Calcium reabsorption in the distal tubule is stimulated by parathyroid hormone.

cards.q: What is the primary metabolic action of cortisol?
cards.a: It raises plasma glucose by stimulating gluconeogenesis.
options: It lowers plasma glucose by increasing muscle uptake
It raises plasma calcium by stimulating bone resorption
It raises plasma sodium by acting on the distal nephron
It raises plasma glucose by stimulating gluconeogenesis
cards.explanation: Cortisol supplies the liver with amino acids and turns on the gluconeogenic enzymes, so plasma glucose is defended during stress and fasting. Lowering glucose by increasing muscle uptake is the action of insulin, the opposing signal. Sodium retention is the aldosterone action, although very high cortisol can spill over onto that receptor. Raising plasma calcium through bone resorption is parathyroid hormone territory.

cards.q: From what molecule are all three classes of adrenal cortical hormone built?
cards.a: Cholesterol.
options: Cholesterol
Tyrosine
Tryptophan
A chain of amino acids
cards.explanation: Aldosterone, cortisol, and the adrenal androgens are all steroids, and every steroid begins as cholesterol before enzymes in each zone modify it. Tyrosine is the precursor of the catecholamines and of thyroid hormone. Tryptophan is the precursor of serotonin and melatonin. A chain of amino acids describes peptide hormones such as insulin and ADH.

cards.q: Which two signals are the main regulators of aldosterone secretion?
cards.a: Angiotensin II and plasma potassium.
options: ACTH and plasma sodium concentration
Angiotensin II and plasma potassium
ADH and total plasma osmolarity
Renin and the plasma glucose level
cards.explanation: The zona glomerulosa responds mainly to angiotensin II generated when blood pressure or volume falls, and directly to a rise in plasma potassium. ACTH has only a small permissive effect on this zone, and plasma sodium is a weak signal compared with these two. ADH and osmolarity control water handling through a separate pathway. Renin acts upstream by generating angiotensin, and plasma glucose is not an input here.

cards.q: Which cortical zones are the main targets of ACTH?
cards.a: The zona fasciculata and zona reticularis.
options: The zona glomerulosa acting alone
All three cortical zones equally
The zona fasciculata and zona reticularis
The zona glomerulosa and the medulla
cards.explanation: ACTH drives cortisol from the fasciculata and androgens from the reticularis, which is why both fall together when ACTH is lost. The glomerulosa keeps working largely without ACTH because it answers to angiotensin II and potassium. Equal control of all three zones would mean losing ACTH also abolishes aldosterone, which does not happen. The medulla is controlled by sympathetic preganglionic neurons, not by ACTH.

cards.q: Plasma aldosterone rises sharply. What happens to plasma potassium?
cards.a: It falls, because more potassium is secreted into the urine.
options: It rises, because potassium follows sodium into the blood
It falls, because potassium is shifted into bone
It is unchanged, because aldosterone only moves sodium
It falls, because more potassium is secreted into the urine
cards.explanation: Aldosterone drives sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion at the same site, so more aldosterone means more potassium lost in the urine and a lower plasma level. Potassium moves opposite to sodium here, not with it. Aldosterone handles both ions, so no change is not the outcome. Bone is a calcium and phosphate store and does not buffer potassium in this way.

cards.q: A person loses blood volume during surgery. Trace the change to the zona glomerulosa.
cards.a: Renin rises, angiotensin II rises, and aldosterone secretion increases.
options: Renin rises, angiotensin II rises, and aldosterone secretion increases
Renin falls, angiotensin II falls, and aldosterone secretion increases
ACTH rises and aldosterone secretion increases with cortisol
Plasma potassium falls and aldosterone secretion increases
cards.explanation: Reduced renal perfusion makes the kidney release renin, angiotensin II is generated, and it stimulates the glomerulosa to release aldosterone so sodium and therefore water are conserved. Falling renin cannot raise aldosterone, since it is the first step of the pathway. ACTH is not the main driver of the glomerulosa. Falling potassium reduces aldosterone rather than increasing it.

cards.q: The entire adrenal cortex is destroyed by autoimmune disease. Predict plasma sodium, plasma potassium, and blood pressure.
cards.a: Sodium low, potassium high, blood pressure low.
options: Sodium high, potassium low, blood pressure high
Sodium low, potassium high, blood pressure low
Sodium low, potassium low, blood pressure high
Sodium high, potassium high, blood pressure low
cards.explanation: Losing aldosterone means sodium is wasted in the urine and potassium is retained, and the sodium loss takes water with it so volume and pressure fall. High sodium with low potassium is the pattern of aldosterone excess, the opposite problem. Low potassium cannot occur when the hormone that excretes it is gone. High sodium with high potassium does not fit a single failing pathway.

cards.q: A patient has had very high ACTH for months. Which change in the adrenal gland do you predict?
cards.a: The zona fasciculata thickens and cortisol output rises.
options: The zona glomerulosa thickens and aldosterone output rises
The adrenal medulla enlarges and epinephrine output rises
The zona fasciculata thickens and cortisol output rises
The whole gland shrinks from overuse
cards.explanation: ACTH is both a secretory signal and a growth signal for the fasciculata, so chronic elevation makes that zone hypertrophy while cortisol output climbs. The glomerulosa is driven by angiotensin II and potassium, so it grows little under ACTH. The medulla answers to sympathetic nerves, not to ACTH. Glands enlarge under chronic trophic stimulation rather than shrinking.

cards.q: A seven year old girl has adrenal androgen secretion many times the normal level. What do you predict?
cards.a: Early appearance of pubic hair and other androgen driven features.
options: Weight gain with a low blood glucose between meals
Delayed puberty with short stature and absent pubic hair
Salt wasting with a low blood pressure and a high plasma potassium
Early appearance of pubic hair and other androgen driven features
cards.explanation: Adrenal androgens are weak but at high concentration they produce the androgen dependent changes of puberty, so signs appear years early. Delayed puberty would follow from too little sex steroid, not too much. Salt wasting comes from aldosterone deficiency, a different zone. Weight gain with low glucose does not fit an androgen excess.

cards.q: A small tumor of the zona glomerulosa secretes aldosterone continuously. Predict blood pressure and plasma potassium.
cards.a: Blood pressure high and potassium low.
options: Blood pressure high and potassium low
Blood pressure low and potassium high
Blood pressure high and potassium high
Blood pressure normal and potassium low
cards.explanation: Continuous aldosterone retains sodium and water, raising volume and pressure, while potassium is steadily secreted into the urine and falls. Low pressure with high potassium is the deficiency picture. Potassium cannot rise while the hormone that excretes it is in excess. Blood pressure does not stay normal when sodium retention is sustained for weeks.

cards.q: A drug blocks the aldosterone receptor in the distal nephron. Predict urinary sodium and urinary potassium.
cards.a: Sodium excretion rises and potassium excretion falls.
options: Sodium excretion falls and potassium excretion rises
Sodium excretion rises and potassium excretion falls
Both sodium and potassium excretion rise
Both sodium and potassium excretion fall
cards.explanation: Blocking the receptor removes the signal to reabsorb sodium and to secrete potassium, so sodium leaves in the urine while potassium is retained in the body. Falling sodium excretion with rising potassium excretion is what aldosterone itself does, not what a blocker does. The two ions move in opposite directions at this site, so both cannot rise or both fall.

cards.q: A patient has high plasma aldosterone and very low plasma renin. What does the renin value tell you?
cards.a: The adrenal gland is secreting on its own rather than responding to the kidney.
options: The kidney is driving aldosterone secretion through angiotensin II release
The patient is volume depleted and the kidney is compensating for that
The adrenal gland is secreting on its own rather than responding to the kidney
The pituitary is secreting excess ACTH and driving the entire cortex hard
cards.explanation: If the kidney were driving the gland, renin would be high, so a suppressed renin with high aldosterone means the adrenal source is autonomous and the resulting volume expansion has shut renin off. Angiotensin II driven secretion requires high renin by definition. Volume depletion raises renin rather than suppressing it. Excess ACTH would raise cortisol and androgens rather than aldosterone.

cards.q: An inherited enzyme defect blocks the final step of cortisol synthesis. Trace what happens to ACTH and to the adrenal androgens.
cards.a: ACTH rises without feedback restraint and androgens increase.
options: ACTH falls and adrenal androgen output falls with it
ACTH is unchanged because cortisol is not its only signal
ACTH rises and all three steroid classes fall together
ACTH rises without feedback restraint and androgens increase
cards.explanation: Cortisol is the negative feedback signal, so if it cannot be made, ACTH climbs, the cortex is driven hard, and the precursors that accumulate are pushed down the androgen pathway that is still intact. ACTH cannot fall when its inhibitor is missing. Androgens rise rather than fall because their pathway is not blocked. Cortisol is the dominant feedback signal for ACTH, so the level does change.

cards.q: A patient with primary adrenal failure has darkened skin creases. Trace the connection.
cards.a: Low cortisol removes feedback, ACTH rises, and ACTH acts on pigment cells.
options: Low cortisol removes feedback, ACTH rises, and ACTH acts on pigment cells
Low aldosterone raises plasma potassium, which darkens the skin creases
High cortisol thins the skin and makes surface vessels more visible
Low adrenal androgens allow melanin to accumulate in skin creases
cards.explanation: When the gland cannot make cortisol, the pituitary loses its brake and pours out ACTH, which acts on melanocytes and deepens pigmentation in creases and scars. Potassium has no effect on skin pigment. High cortisol thins skin but that is the excess state, not adrenal failure. Adrenal androgens do not restrain melanin production.

cards.q: Two patients each lack one cortical hormone. Patient A lacks aldosterone only, patient B lacks cortisol only. Which finding separates them?
cards.a: Patient A has high plasma potassium, patient B has low fasting glucose.
options: Patient A has low fasting glucose, patient B has high plasma potassium
Patient A has high plasma potassium, patient B has low fasting glucose
Both have high plasma potassium but only A has low glucose
Both have low fasting glucose but only B has high potassium
cards.explanation: Aldosterone controls sodium and potassium handling, so losing it raises plasma potassium, while cortisol defends glucose during fasting, so losing it lets fasting glucose fall. The reversed pairing assigns each problem to the wrong hormone. Neither patient should show both defects, because each lacks only one hormone and the two zones act on different systems.

cards.q: What does cortisol do to hepatic gluconeogenesis?
cards.a: It increases it.
options: It increases it
It decreases it
It leaves it unchanged
It increases it only when insulin is also high
cards.explanation: Cortisol turns on the liver enzymes that build glucose from amino acids and glycerol, which is how it defends plasma glucose during a prolonged stress or fast. Decreasing gluconeogenesis is what insulin does. Leaving it unchanged would remove the main metabolic reason cortisol matters. High insulin opposes the effect rather than being required for it.

cards.q: What is the effect of cortisol on skeletal muscle protein?
cards.a: It breaks protein down and releases amino acids.
options: It builds protein and increases muscle mass
It breaks protein down and releases amino acids
It has no effect on muscle protein
It traps amino acids inside muscle cells
cards.explanation: Cortisol is catabolic in muscle, freeing amino acids that travel to the liver as raw material for glucose synthesis. Building muscle protein is what growth hormone and insulin do. No effect would leave the muscle wasting of chronic cortisol excess unexplained. Trapping amino acids inside the cell is the opposite of the export that gluconeogenesis requires.

cards.q: What is the effect of cortisol on the immune response?
cards.a: It suppresses it.
options: It enhances it
It has no effect on it
It suppresses it
It enhances it only during acute stress
cards.explanation: Cortisol reduces circulating lymphocytes, damps cytokine production, and blunts inflammation, which is why glucocorticoid drugs are used to control immune reactions. Enhancing immunity is the opposite of the observed effect. No effect would make glucocorticoids useless as anti inflammatory agents. Even acute stress cortisol suppresses rather than enhances the response.

cards.q: How does cortisol support blood pressure?
cards.a: It permits vascular smooth muscle to respond fully to catecholamines.
options: It directly constricts arterioles on its own without help
It causes the adrenal medulla to release more epinephrine
It increases the heart rate through beta receptors it activates itself
It permits vascular smooth muscle to respond fully to catecholamines
cards.explanation: Cortisol is permissive, meaning it maintains the receptors and signaling that let norepinephrine and epinephrine constrict vessels, so without it the same catecholamine level produces a much weaker response. Cortisol does not itself bind vascular receptors to constrict. It does not activate beta receptors on the heart. Medullary catecholamine release is driven by sympathetic nerves rather than by cortisol.

cards.q: At what time of day is plasma cortisol normally highest?
cards.a: Early morning, around waking.
options: Early morning, around waking
Late evening, before sleep
Immediately after the largest meal
It is constant throughout the day
cards.explanation: Cortisol follows a daily rhythm with a peak just before and around waking, which prepares fuel mobilization for the day ahead. Late evening is the trough, when levels are lowest. Meals influence insulin and glucagon far more than cortisol. A constant level would mean there was no rhythm, which is not the case.

cards.q: What is the correct order of the hormones in the stress axis?
cards.a: CRH, then ACTH, then cortisol.
options: ACTH, then CRH, then cortisol
CRH, then ACTH, then cortisol
CRH, then cortisol, then ACTH
ACTH, then cortisol, then CRH
cards.explanation: The hypothalamus releases corticotropin releasing hormone into the portal blood, the anterior pituitary responds with ACTH, and the adrenal cortex responds with cortisol. Any ordering that puts ACTH before CRH reverses the brain to pituitary step. Cortisol is always the final output, since it comes from the target gland at the end of the chain.

cards.q: Where does cortisol exert its negative feedback?
cards.a: On the hypothalamus and the anterior pituitary.
options: On the cells of the adrenal cortex itself
On the posterior pituitary and its terminals
On the hypothalamus and the anterior pituitary
On the liver and on skeletal muscle cells
cards.explanation: Cortisol inhibits CRH release from the hypothalamus and ACTH release from the anterior pituitary, closing the loop at both levels above the gland. Feedback onto the adrenal cortex itself is not the main mechanism, since the cortex only responds to the ACTH it receives. The posterior pituitary handles ADH and oxytocin. Liver and muscle are target tissues for the metabolic actions, not feedback sites.

cards.q: What does cortisol do to adipose tissue?
cards.a: It promotes lipolysis and releases fatty acids.
options: It blocks fatty acid release during fasting
It promotes triglyceride storage in the limbs
It converts fat cells into muscle cells
It promotes lipolysis and releases fatty acids
cards.explanation: Cortisol frees fatty acids from stored triglyceride so tissues can burn fat while glucose is reserved, which is part of its fuel mobilizing role. Storage in the limbs is not a cortisol effect, and chronic excess actually thins the limbs. Fat cells cannot become muscle cells. Blocking fatty acid release during fasting would work against the purpose of the hormone.

cards.q: A person has eaten nothing for 36 hours. How does cortisol help keep plasma glucose from falling?
cards.a: By supplying amino acids from muscle for hepatic glucose synthesis.
options: By supplying amino acids from muscle for hepatic glucose synthesis
By increasing glucose uptake into muscle and fat tissue
By stimulating insulin release from the pancreatic beta cells
By preventing the brain from taking up glucose from the blood
cards.explanation: Cortisol breaks down muscle protein and the released amino acids become substrate for gluconeogenesis, so the liver can keep glucose in the blood well past the point where glycogen runs out. Increasing muscle uptake would lower plasma glucose, which is backwards. Insulin release falls during a fast rather than being stimulated by cortisol. Brain glucose uptake is insulin independent and is not blocked.

cards.q: A patient takes high dose glucocorticoid medication daily for a year. Predict plasma ACTH and adrenal size.
cards.a: ACTH low and the adrenal cortex atrophied.
options: ACTH high and the adrenal cortex enlarged
ACTH low and the adrenal cortex atrophied
ACTH low and the adrenal cortex enlarged
ACTH high and the adrenal cortex atrophied
cards.explanation: The drug acts like cortisol at the feedback sites, so ACTH is suppressed, and without its trophic signal the fasciculata shrinks over months. High ACTH would require the feedback signal to be absent. An enlarged cortex needs ACTH stimulation, which is exactly what is missing. High ACTH with an atrophied cortex would describe a gland that cannot respond, not a suppressed axis.

cards.q: Why do patients on long term high dose glucocorticoids get infections more easily?
cards.a: Cortisol suppresses lymphocyte function and the inflammatory response.
options: Cortisol reduces the number of red blood cells in the circulation
Cortisol thins the blood and spreads the bacteria more quickly
Cortisol suppresses lymphocyte function and the inflammatory response
Cortisol lowers body temperature so that bacteria grow much better
cards.explanation: Fewer and less active lymphocytes plus a blunted inflammatory response mean an invading organism meets weaker resistance and infections both start more easily and are noticed later. Red cell number is not meaningfully reduced by cortisol. Cortisol does not change blood viscosity in a way that spreads infection. Body temperature is not lowered enough to favor bacterial growth.

cards.q: How does chronic cortisol excess affect bone?
cards.a: Bone density falls because formation is suppressed and absorption drops.
options: Bone density rises because dietary protein is redirected to bone
Bone density falls because parathyroid hormone secretion stops entirely
Bone density is unchanged because bone is not a cortisol target tissue
Bone density falls because formation is suppressed and absorption drops
cards.explanation: Cortisol inhibits osteoblasts and reduces intestinal calcium absorption while increasing urinary calcium loss, so the balance tips toward bone loss over months. Bone gain would require an anabolic signal, and cortisol is catabolic. Bone is very much a cortisol target, which is why osteoporosis is a well known consequence. Parathyroid hormone does not stop, and if anything it rises in response to the calcium losses.

cards.q: A patient with chronic cortisol excess has thin arms and legs but increased fat over the trunk and face. Which cortisol action explains the thin limbs?
cards.a: Breakdown of skeletal muscle protein in the limbs.
options: Breakdown of skeletal muscle protein in the limbs
Reduced blood flow to the muscles of the limbs
Loss of subcutaneous fat only from the limbs
Failure of growth hormone secretion from the pituitary
cards.explanation: Cortisol is catabolic in skeletal muscle, and since the limbs are mostly muscle they visibly waste while fat is redistributed toward the trunk and face. Blood flow to the limbs is not meaningfully reduced by cortisol. Fat loss alone would not produce the weakness that goes with this pattern. Growth hormone secretion is somewhat blunted but muscle catabolism is the direct explanation.

cards.q: What does cortisol do to glucose uptake in muscle and fat, and how does that interact with insulin?
cards.a: It reduces uptake, so insulin has to work against it.
options: It increases uptake, adding to the insulin effect
It reduces uptake, so insulin has to work against it
It has no effect on uptake but blocks insulin secretion
It reduces uptake by destroying the insulin receptor permanently
cards.explanation: Cortisol makes muscle and fat less responsive to insulin, so glucose is left in the blood for the brain, and the beta cells must secrete more insulin to achieve the same effect. Adding to the insulin effect would lower glucose, which is the opposite of what cortisol does. Cortisol does not block insulin secretion, and beta cells usually increase output. The receptor is not destroyed, and the resistance reverses when cortisol falls.

cards.q: A patient is given a glucocorticoid for a severe inflammatory reaction. What change in the inflamed tissue do you predict?
cards.a: Less swelling, redness, and immune cell infiltration.
options: More swelling as fluid is drawn into the tissue
No change, because cortisol acts only on metabolism
Less swelling, redness, and immune cell infiltration
Faster wound closure with stronger scar tissue
cards.explanation: Glucocorticoids reduce cytokine production and limit the migration of immune cells into tissue, so the visible signs of inflammation subside. More swelling would be the response to a pro inflammatory signal. Cortisol has broad immune actions in addition to metabolic ones. Healing is actually slowed and scar tissue weakened, which is a cost of the treatment.

cards.q: A patient on daily glucocorticoids for a year stops the drug abruptly and becomes hypotensive and hypoglycemic. Trace the mechanism.
cards.a: The suppressed adrenal cortex has atrophied and cannot supply cortisol.
options: The drug is still circulating and is blocking the cortisol receptors
Aldosterone is lost first, and cortisol levels stay entirely normal
ACTH secretion rises too fast and overwhelms the adrenal gland
The suppressed adrenal cortex has atrophied and cannot supply cortisol
cards.explanation: A year of feedback suppression shrinks the fasciculata, so when the outside supply is removed the gland cannot restart in time, and the loss of cortisol removes both the permissive support for blood pressure and the drive for gluconeogenesis. A stopped drug is cleared rather than left blocking receptors. Rising ACTH is the recovery signal, not the cause of collapse. Aldosterone comes from the glomerulosa, which is not suppressed by the drug in the same way.

cards.q: A student sleeps poorly and is under heavy pressure for months. Predict the combined effect on plasma glucose, infection risk, and blood pressure.
cards.a: Glucose higher, infection risk higher, blood pressure higher.
options: Glucose higher, infection risk higher, blood pressure higher
Glucose lower, infection risk higher, blood pressure lower
Glucose higher, infection risk lower, blood pressure higher
Glucose lower, infection risk lower, blood pressure lower
cards.explanation: Sustained cortisol raises glucose through gluconeogenesis and insulin resistance, suppresses immune defense so infections take hold more easily, and supports vascular tone so pressure drifts upward. Lower glucose would require cortisol to act like insulin. Reduced infection risk contradicts the immune suppression. All three moving downward describes cortisol deficiency instead.

cards.q: A healthy person is given a small dose of a synthetic glucocorticoid at night. What is measured the next morning, and why?
cards.a: Cortisol is low, because the drug fed back on the pituitary.
options: Cortisol is high, because the drug adds to the normal morning peak
Cortisol is low, because the drug fed back on the pituitary
Cortisol is unchanged, because feedback needs several days to act
ACTH is high, because the drug directly stimulates the pituitary
cards.explanation: The synthetic steroid is read by the feedback receptors as cortisol, so CRH and ACTH are shut down overnight and the adrenal makes little cortisol of its own by morning. The drug does not add to measured cortisol, since the assay reports the natural hormone. Feedback works within hours, not days. ACTH is suppressed rather than stimulated by a glucocorticoid.

cards.q: A patient with adrenal insufficiency has normal plasma epinephrine and norepinephrine but still has a low blood pressure that responds poorly to those hormones. Explain.
cards.a: Without cortisol the vessels lose their permissive support and respond weakly.
options: The catecholamines are being broken down before they reach the vessels
The vessels are already maximally constricted, so no further effect is possible
Without cortisol the vessels lose their permissive support and respond weakly
Aldosterone is normal, so the low pressure must be a measurement error
cards.explanation: Cortisol maintains the receptors and signaling machinery that let catecholamines constrict arterioles, so when it is missing a normal catecholamine level produces an abnormally small response, which is what permissive means. Accelerated breakdown would show up as low measured catecholamine levels. Maximal constriction would give a high pressure, not a low one. Aldosterone is usually low as well in adrenal insufficiency, and the low pressure is real.

cards.q: Which cells sense a fall in plasma calcium and respond by secreting a hormone?
cards.a: Parathyroid chief cells.
options: Thyroid follicular cells
Parathyroid chief cells
Parafollicular C cells
Adrenal glomerulosa cells
cards.explanation: Chief cells of the parathyroid glands carry a calcium sensing receptor, and when plasma calcium drops they increase parathyroid hormone secretion within minutes. Thyroid follicular cells make T3 and T4 and do not monitor calcium. Parafollicular C cells sense a rise in calcium and release calcitonin instead. Adrenal glomerulosa cells respond to angiotensin II and potassium.

cards.q: What is the overall effect of parathyroid hormone on plasma calcium?
cards.a: It raises plasma calcium.
options: It raises plasma calcium only when vitamin D is absent
It lowers plasma calcium
It raises plasma calcium
It has no direct effect on plasma calcium
cards.explanation: Parathyroid hormone is the main defender of plasma calcium and raises it by acting on bone, kidney, and indirectly on intestine. Lowering plasma calcium is what calcitonin does. Vitamin D assists rather than opposes the hormone, so its absence weakens the response rather than being required for it. The effect on plasma calcium is the reason the hormone exists.

cards.q: What does parathyroid hormone do in bone?
cards.a: It increases osteoclast resorption, releasing calcium into the blood.
options: It increases osteoblast activity, adding new calcium to the bone
It blocks calcium from leaving the bone matrix altogether
It converts cartilage into bone at the epiphyseal growth plate
It increases osteoclast resorption, releasing calcium into the blood
cards.explanation: Parathyroid hormone drives bone resorption, and osteoclasts dissolve mineral and release both calcium and phosphate into the blood, which is the fastest large store the body can draw on. Increasing osteoblast deposition would remove calcium from the plasma instead. Endochondral growth at the plate is driven by growth hormone and IGF-1. Blocking calcium exit from bone would defeat the purpose of the hormone.

cards.q: What does parathyroid hormone do to calcium handling in the kidney?
cards.a: It increases calcium reabsorption in the distal tubule.
options: It increases calcium reabsorption in the distal tubule
It increases calcium excretion into the urine instead
It increases calcium filtration at the glomerulus
It has no action on calcium anywhere in the nephron
cards.explanation: Parathyroid hormone makes the distal tubule reclaim more filtered calcium, so less is lost in the urine and plasma calcium is defended. Increasing excretion would work against the hormone's purpose. Filtration at the glomerulus depends on the plasma concentration and pressure, not on this hormone. The renal action is one of the three arms of the response, so it cannot be absent.

cards.q: What does parathyroid hormone do to phosphate handling in the kidney?
cards.a: It decreases phosphate reabsorption, so more is excreted.
options: It increases phosphate reabsorption along with that of calcium
It decreases phosphate reabsorption, so more is excreted
It has no effect at all on renal phosphate handling
It decreases phosphate excretion, raising plasma phosphate
cards.explanation: Parathyroid hormone inhibits phosphate reabsorption in the proximal tubule, so plasma phosphate falls even while calcium rises, which keeps the two ions from precipitating together in tissue. Reabsorbing both would raise the calcium phosphate product and risk deposits. No effect would leave the low plasma phosphate of hyperparathyroidism unexplained. Reduced excretion is the opposite of what the hormone does.

cards.q: Which organ carries out the final activation step that produces calcitriol?
cards.a: The kidney.
options: The liver
The small intestine
The kidney
The parathyroid gland
cards.explanation: The kidney holds the 1 alpha hydroxylase enzyme that converts the inactive precursor into calcitriol, and parathyroid hormone turns that enzyme on. The liver performs an earlier hydroxylation but not the activating step. The small intestine is the target of calcitriol rather than its source. The parathyroid gland makes the hormone that triggers the conversion, not the vitamin itself.

cards.q: What is the main action of calcitriol?
cards.a: It increases calcium absorption from the intestine.
options: It increases calcium secretion into the gut lumen
It increases calcium loss in the urine
It stops osteoclasts from resorbing bone
It increases calcium absorption from the intestine
cards.explanation: Calcitriol acts on intestinal cells to build the transport proteins that carry dietary calcium into the blood, which is the only route by which the body gains new calcium. Increasing urinary loss would lower plasma calcium. Stopping osteoclasts is closer to what calcitonin does. Secretion into the gut lumen is the opposite direction from absorption.

cards.q: Which cells secrete calcitonin, and what does it do?
cards.a: Parafollicular C cells of the thyroid, and it lowers plasma calcium.
options: Parafollicular C cells of the thyroid, and it lowers plasma calcium
Parathyroid chief cells, and it lowers plasma calcium
Thyroid follicular cells, and it raises plasma calcium
Parafollicular C cells of the thyroid, and it raises plasma calcium
cards.explanation: Calcitonin comes from the parafollicular C cells scattered between thyroid follicles and it inhibits osteoclasts, which lowers plasma calcium. Chief cells of the parathyroid secrete parathyroid hormone, the opposing signal. Follicular cells make T3 and T4. Calcitonin lowers rather than raises plasma calcium, which is the point of having it.

cards.q: Plasma calcium falls from 10 to 8 mg/dL. What happens to parathyroid hormone secretion?
cards.a: It increases within minutes.
options: It decreases within minutes
It increases within minutes
It is unchanged until calcium falls below 6 mg/dL
It increases only after calcitriol rises first
cards.explanation: The calcium sensing receptor on chief cells detects small drops and releases the brake on secretion, so parathyroid hormone rises quickly and begins correcting the fall. A decrease would let the fall continue unopposed. The system responds to small deviations rather than waiting for a severe one. Calcitriol rises as a result of parathyroid hormone, not before it.

cards.q: Parathyroid hormone raises intestinal calcium absorption even though the intestine has no parathyroid hormone receptors. How?
cards.a: It stimulates the kidney to make calcitriol, which acts on the intestine.
options: It reaches the intestine through the portal vein at higher concentration
It stimulates the liver to release calcium binding protein into the gut
It stimulates the kidney to make calcitriol, which acts on the intestine
It stimulates calcitonin, which then acts on the intestine
cards.explanation: The intestinal arm of the response is indirect, since parathyroid hormone turns on renal 1 alpha hydroxylase and it is calcitriol that induces the intestinal calcium transporters. The liver does not release a calcium binding protein into the gut for this purpose. Portal blood carries absorbed nutrients away from the gut, not hormone toward it. Calcitonin opposes parathyroid hormone and does not mediate its actions.

cards.q: The parathyroid glands are removed. Predict plasma calcium and the effect on nerve and muscle.
cards.a: Calcium falls and nerve and muscle become more excitable.
options: Calcium rises and nerve and muscle become less excitable
Calcium falls and nerve and muscle become less excitable
Calcium rises and nerve and muscle become more excitable
Calcium falls and nerve and muscle become more excitable
cards.explanation: Without parathyroid hormone plasma calcium falls, and low extracellular calcium makes voltage gated sodium channels open more readily, so nerves fire spontaneously and muscles go into tetany. Reduced excitability with low calcium is the opposite of what is observed. Calcium cannot rise when the hormone that defends it is gone. High calcium is what makes tissue less excitable, and that is the other end of the range.

cards.q: A person gets almost no vitamin D and little sunlight for two years. Predict intestinal calcium absorption and the state of bone.
cards.a: Absorption falls and bone becomes poorly mineralized.
options: Absorption falls and bone becomes poorly mineralized
