Absorption rises and the bone becomes denser
Absorption falls and the bone becomes denser
Absorption is unchanged and bone mineral is unaffected
cards.explanation: Without calcitriol the intestine cannot take up dietary calcium efficiently, so parathyroid hormone rises and draws calcium out of bone to hold the plasma level, leaving bone soft and undermineralized. Absorption cannot rise when the hormone that drives it is missing. Bone loses mineral rather than gaining it under this pressure. No change would contradict the requirement for vitamin D in calcium uptake.

cards.q: A patient in chronic kidney failure cannot make calcitriol. What happens to plasma calcium and parathyroid hormone?
cards.a: Calcium falls and parathyroid hormone rises.
options: Calcium rises and parathyroid hormone falls
Calcium falls and parathyroid hormone rises
Calcium falls and parathyroid hormone falls
Calcium rises and parathyroid hormone rises
cards.explanation: Losing calcitriol cuts intestinal calcium uptake, plasma calcium drifts down, and the parathyroid glands respond by secreting more hormone in a sustained attempt to correct it. Rising calcium would require the intestinal arm to be intact. Parathyroid hormone cannot fall while calcium is low, because the calcium sensing receptor drives it up. Calcium and parathyroid hormone rising together would point to an autonomous gland, not to kidney failure.

cards.q: Plasma calcium rises well above normal after a large calcium infusion. What happens to calcitonin?
cards.a: Calcitonin secretion increases.
options: Calcitonin secretion is unchanged
Calcitonin secretion decreases
Calcitonin secretion increases
Calcitonin is converted to parathyroid hormone
cards.explanation: Parafollicular C cells respond to a high plasma calcium by releasing calcitonin, which inhibits osteoclasts and slows calcium entry into the blood. A decrease would be the response to low calcium. No change would leave the C cells without a function. Calcitonin and parathyroid hormone are different peptides from different glands and are not interconverted.

cards.q: Why does a person with very low plasma calcium develop muscle spasms?
cards.a: Low extracellular calcium lowers the threshold for firing an action potential.
options: Low extracellular calcium raises the resting membrane potential above threshold
Low extracellular calcium increases calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum
Low extracellular calcium prevents muscle relaxation after contraction
Low extracellular calcium lowers the threshold for firing an action potential
cards.explanation: Extracellular calcium normally stabilizes the membrane by making sodium channels harder to open, so when it falls the channels open at less depolarization and nerves fire on their own, driving the muscle into spasm. Sarcoplasmic reticulum stores are not increased by low plasma calcium. Relaxation depends on pumping calcium back into the reticulum and is not what fails here. The resting potential is not driven above threshold, since the change is in threshold rather than in the resting value.

cards.q: A patient has a parathyroid tumor secreting hormone continuously. Predict plasma calcium, plasma phosphate, and the state of bone.
cards.a: Calcium high, phosphate low, bone resorbed.
options: Calcium high, phosphate low, bone resorbed
Calcium high, phosphate high, bone resorbed
Calcium low, phosphate high, bone dense
Calcium high, phosphate low, bone dense
cards.explanation: Continuous parathyroid hormone drives bone resorption and renal calcium reabsorption so plasma calcium climbs, while the same hormone blocks phosphate reabsorption so phosphate is wasted in the urine and falls. High phosphate would require the renal phosphate action to be absent. Low calcium contradicts an excess of the hormone that raises it. Bone cannot become denser while resorption is being driven hard.

cards.q: Plasma calcium falls after a low calcium meal. Trace the full corrective response through all three target organs.
cards.a: Parathyroid hormone rises, bone resorption and renal reabsorption rise, and calcitriol aids absorption.
options: Calcitonin rises, bone resorption rises, and intestinal calcium absorption rises
Parathyroid hormone rises, bone resorption and renal reabsorption rise, and calcitriol aids absorption
Parathyroid hormone rises, bone formation rises, and renal calcium excretion rises steadily as well
Calcitriol rises first, which then stimulates parathyroid hormone release and bone resorption in turn
cards.explanation: The corrective loop has three arms, all triggered by parathyroid hormone: calcium is pulled from bone within hours, less is lost in the urine, and over a day or two calcitriol made in the kidney increases uptake from food. Calcitonin lowers calcium and would worsen the fall. Increasing bone formation and urinary excretion would both remove calcium from plasma. Calcitriol is produced in response to parathyroid hormone, so it does not come first.

cards.q: A woman eats a calcium poor diet for years yet her plasma calcium stays normal at every check. What has been sacrificed to keep it there?
cards.a: Bone mineral, which has been resorbed to supply the plasma.
options: Intestinal transport proteins, which have been used up
Renal filtration, which has been reduced to save calcium
Bone mineral, which has been resorbed to supply the plasma
Parathyroid tissue, which has been exhausted by long use
cards.explanation: Plasma calcium is defended tightly because nerve and muscle depend on it, and the skeleton is the reservoir the body draws on, so a normal plasma value over years of poor intake usually means bone has been mined. Transport proteins are made continuously under calcitriol and are not depleted. Filtration rate is not reduced to conserve calcium. The parathyroid glands enlarge under chronic demand rather than becoming exhausted.

cards.q: Two days after a thyroid operation a patient has tingling around the mouth and cramping in the hands. Which mechanism explains this best?
cards.a: The parathyroid glands were injured, so plasma calcium fell.
options: Thyroid hormone was removed, so metabolic rate fell
Plasma phosphate fell, which made nerves fire spontaneously
Calcitonin secretion rose sharply after the operation
The parathyroid glands were injured, so plasma calcium fell
cards.explanation: The parathyroid glands sit on the back of the thyroid and are easily damaged during thyroid surgery, and losing parathyroid hormone drops plasma calcium enough to cause the tingling and tetany of increased nerve excitability. A low metabolic rate from lost thyroid hormone develops over weeks and causes sluggishness rather than tetany. Calcitonin is lost rather than raised when thyroid tissue is removed. A low phosphate does not by itself produce tetany, and here phosphate would rise as parathyroid hormone falls.

cards.q: Which islet cell secretes insulin?
cards.a: The beta cell.
options: The alpha cell
The delta cell
The beta cell
The acinar cell
cards.explanation: Beta cells make up the bulk of each pancreatic islet and are the only source of insulin. Alpha cells secrete glucagon, the hormone that opposes insulin. Delta cells secrete somatostatin, which damps both. Acinar cells are exocrine and release digestive enzymes into the duct system rather than hormones into the blood.

cards.q: Which islet cell secretes glucagon?
cards.a: The alpha cell.
options: The parafollicular cell
The beta cell
The delta cell
The alpha cell
cards.explanation: Alpha cells sit at the periphery of the islet and release glucagon when plasma glucose falls. Beta cells release insulin, which acts in the opposite direction. Delta cells release somatostatin. Parafollicular cells belong to the thyroid and secrete calcitonin, so they are not part of the pancreas at all.

cards.q: What is the main stimulus for insulin secretion?
cards.a: A rise in plasma glucose.
options: A rise in plasma glucose
A fall in plasma glucose
A rise in plasma potassium
A fall in plasma amino acids
cards.explanation: Beta cells take up and metabolize glucose, and the resulting rise in ATP closes potassium channels and triggers insulin release, so plasma glucose is the direct stimulus. A fall in glucose is the signal for glucagon instead. Plasma potassium regulates aldosterone. Amino acids stimulate insulin when they rise, not when they fall.

cards.q: What is the main stimulus for glucagon secretion?
cards.a: A fall in plasma glucose.
options: A rise in plasma glucose
A fall in plasma glucose
A rise in plasma insulin alone
A rise in plasma calcium
cards.explanation: Alpha cells respond to a falling plasma glucose by releasing glucagon so the liver can put glucose back into the blood. A rising glucose suppresses glucagon and stimulates insulin. Insulin does inhibit alpha cells, but it is the glucose level rather than insulin alone that is the primary signal. Plasma calcium is monitored by the parathyroid glands.

cards.q: What does insulin do to liver glycogen?
cards.a: It promotes glycogen synthesis and storage.
options: It converts glycogen into fatty acids directly
It promotes glycogen breakdown into glucose
It promotes glycogen synthesis and storage
It blocks glucose from entering the liver at all
cards.explanation: Insulin activates glycogen synthase and inhibits the breakdown enzymes, so after a meal the liver packs glucose away as glycogen. Breaking glycogen down is the glucagon action. Glycogen is not converted straight into fatty acids, although surplus glucose can be used for fat synthesis by a separate route. Hepatic glucose entry is not insulin dependent, which is what lets the liver sense glucose directly.

cards.q: What does glucagon do to liver glycogen?
cards.a: It breaks glycogen down and releases glucose into the blood.
options: It stores glucose as glycogen for later use by the body
It moves glycogen from the liver to skeletal muscle
It converts glycogen into muscle protein for storage
It breaks glycogen down and releases glucose into the blood
cards.explanation: Glucagon activates glycogen phosphorylase in hepatocytes, and because the liver can release free glucose into the blood, plasma glucose rises within minutes. Storing glycogen is the insulin action. Glycogen cannot become protein. Glycogen is not transported between tissues, since each tissue keeps its own store.

cards.q: Which glucose transporter does insulin recruit into the membrane of muscle and fat cells?
cards.a: GLUT4.
options: GLUT4
GLUT2
GLUT1
SGLT1
cards.explanation: Insulin causes vesicles carrying GLUT4 to fuse with the membrane of muscle and adipose cells, which is how it increases glucose uptake in those tissues. GLUT1 provides basal uptake in many cells and is not insulin regulated. GLUT2 is the high capacity transporter in liver and beta cells that lets them sense glucose. SGLT1 is a sodium coupled transporter in the intestine and kidney.

cards.q: Which hormone lowers plasma glucose?
cards.a: Insulin.
options: Glucagon
Insulin
Cortisol
Growth hormone
cards.explanation: Insulin is the only hormone that lowers plasma glucose, which it does by moving glucose into muscle and fat and by driving storage in the liver. Glucagon raises glucose by mobilizing hepatic stores. Cortisol raises it through gluconeogenesis and insulin resistance. Growth hormone also raises it by opposing insulin in muscle and fat.

cards.q: Thirty minutes after a large plate of pasta, what has happened to the insulin to glucagon ratio?
cards.a: It has risen, favoring storage.
options: It is unchanged, since both rise together
It has fallen, favoring mobilization
It has risen, favoring storage
It has risen, favoring hepatic glucose release
cards.explanation: Absorbed glucose raises plasma glucose, which stimulates beta cells and inhibits alpha cells, so the ratio swings toward insulin and the body shifts into storing fuel. A falling ratio is the fasting pattern. The two hormones move in opposite directions rather than together. A high insulin ratio suppresses hepatic glucose release rather than promoting it.

cards.q: A person has not eaten since dinner and wakes at 7 am. Which hormone is holding plasma glucose up, and by what route?
cards.a: Glucagon, through hepatic glycogen breakdown.
options: Insulin, through hepatic glucose uptake
Glucagon, through glucose uptake into muscle
Insulin, through GLUT4 recruitment in muscle
Glucagon, through hepatic glycogen breakdown
cards.explanation: Overnight the plasma glucose drifts down, alpha cells release glucagon, and the liver breaks down glycogen to keep the blood supplied for the brain. Insulin would lower glucose further, which is the wrong direction. GLUT4 recruitment moves glucose out of the blood into muscle. Glucagon does not act on skeletal muscle to take up glucose.

cards.q: A fasting person is given insulin. Predict plasma glucose and the alpha cell response.
cards.a: Glucose falls and glucagon secretion rises.
options: Glucose falls and glucagon secretion rises
Glucose falls and glucagon secretion falls
Glucose rises and glucagon secretion falls
Glucose is unchanged and glucagon secretion rises
cards.explanation: Insulin drives glucose into muscle and fat and stops hepatic output, so plasma glucose drops, and the falling glucose is the very signal that turns on the alpha cells. Glucagon cannot fall while glucose is dropping, since that would remove the defense against hypoglycemia. Glucose cannot rise after insulin is given. An unchanged glucose would mean the insulin had no effect.

cards.q: Besides breaking down glycogen, what else does glucagon do in the liver during a long fast?
cards.a: It drives gluconeogenesis and ketone body formation.
options: It drives triglyceride storage and protein synthesis
It drives gluconeogenesis and ketone body formation
It drives glucose uptake and glycogen storage
It drives conversion of glucose into amino acids
cards.explanation: Once glycogen runs low, glucagon keeps glucose coming by building it from amino acids and glycerol, and it also sends fatty acids down the ketone pathway to supply an alternative fuel. Storage of triglyceride and protein synthesis are insulin driven processes. Glucose uptake and glycogen storage are the opposite of what glucagon does. Glucose is not converted into amino acids in any meaningful amount.

cards.q: An autoimmune process destroys the beta cells but leaves the alpha cells intact. Predict fasting plasma glucose.
cards.a: It rises, because nothing opposes glucagon.
options: It falls, because the islet is damaged
It stays normal, because alpha cells compensate
It rises, because nothing opposes glucagon
It falls, because glucagon secretion also stops
cards.explanation: With no insulin the liver keeps releasing glucose and muscle and fat cannot take it up, so plasma glucose climbs even during a fast. Islet damage that removes insulin raises glucose rather than lowering it. Alpha cells raise glucose, so they cannot compensate for missing insulin. Glucagon secretion continues and in fact rises when insulin is absent.

cards.q: A tumor of the alpha cells secretes glucagon continuously. Predict plasma glucose and liver glycogen stores.
cards.a: Glucose high and glycogen stores depleted.
options: Glucose low and glycogen stores full
Glucose low and glycogen stores depleted
Glucose high and glycogen stores full
Glucose high and glycogen stores depleted
cards.explanation: Continuous glucagon keeps the liver breaking down glycogen and making new glucose, so plasma glucose runs high while the hepatic store is steadily drained. Low glucose with full glycogen is the picture of insulin excess. Glycogen cannot stay full while the hormone that mobilizes it is always on. Glucose does not fall under a hormone whose job is to raise it.

cards.q: During prolonged moderate exercise, plasma glucose starts to drift down. Predict what happens to insulin and glucagon.
cards.a: Insulin falls and glucagon rises.
options: Insulin falls and glucagon rises
Insulin rises and glucagon falls
Both rise to meet the demand for fuel
Both fall because the pancreas is not perfused
cards.explanation: Falling glucose plus sympathetic activity suppresses beta cells and stimulates alpha cells, so the liver releases glucose while working muscle takes it up by a route that does not need insulin. Rising insulin during exercise would drop plasma glucose further. Both rising would send contradictory signals to the liver. Pancreatic perfusion is maintained during exercise, so that is not the reason.

cards.q: Trace the sequence after a carbohydrate meal, from the rise in plasma glucose back to a normal level.
cards.a: Glucose rises, insulin rises, uptake and storage increase, glucose falls, insulin falls.
options: Glucose rises, glucagon rises, hepatic output falls, glucose falls, and glucagon falls
Glucose rises, insulin rises, uptake and storage increase, glucose falls, insulin falls
Insulin rises first, glucose then rises, storage increases, and insulin falls again
Glucose rises, insulin rises, hepatic glucose output rises, and glucose falls
cards.explanation: The loop is a textbook negative feedback: the rise in glucose is the stimulus, insulin is the response, uptake into muscle and fat plus hepatic storage remove the glucose, and as glucose returns to baseline the stimulus for insulin disappears. Glucagon falls after a meal rather than rising. Insulin cannot rise before the glucose that stimulates it. Hepatic glucose output falls under insulin, so it cannot be part of the correction.

cards.q: On the second day of a complete fast, hepatic glycogen is essentially gone. How does glucagon still keep plasma glucose from collapsing?
cards.a: By driving gluconeogenesis from amino acids and glycerol.
options: By slowing glucose uptake into the brain
By converting fatty acids directly into glucose in the liver
By driving gluconeogenesis from amino acids and glycerol
By stimulating the kidney to reabsorb more filtered glucose
cards.explanation: With the glycogen store empty, the liver builds new glucose from amino acids released by muscle and from the glycerol backbone of triglycerides, and glucagon is the signal that keeps those pathways running. Fatty acids cannot be converted into glucose in humans, although their glycerol can. Brain glucose uptake is not hormonally throttled. Filtered glucose is already reabsorbed almost completely at normal plasma levels, so there is nothing extra to reclaim.

cards.q: Somatostatin from the delta cells inhibits both alpha and beta cells. What happens to the glucose response to a meal if somatostatin is high?
cards.a: The rise in glucose is larger and longer, because insulin is blunted.
options: The rise in glucose is smaller, because glucagon is also inhibited here
Glucose falls below the fasting level, because glucagon is inhibited more
Glucose does not rise at all, because intestinal absorption is blocked
The rise in glucose is larger and longer, because insulin is blunted
cards.explanation: After a meal the dominant hormone is insulin, so blunting it matters most and the glucose curve rises higher and returns to baseline more slowly even though glucagon is suppressed too. Suppressing glucagon has little effect right after a meal, when glucagon is already low. Somatostatin does slow gastric emptying but absorption still occurs. Glucose does not fall below fasting when the main lowering hormone is inhibited.

cards.q: A person injects their usual insulin dose and then skips the meal. Trace what happens over the next two hours.
cards.a: Glucose falls, glucagon rises, and the liver releases glucose in defense.
options: Glucose falls, glucagon rises, and the liver releases glucose in defense
Glucose rises, insulin is used up, and glucagon secretion falls
Glucose falls, and insulin secretion from the beta cells increases further
Glucose stays normal, because injected insulin acts only after a meal
cards.explanation: Injected insulin drives glucose into muscle and fat with no meal to replace it, so plasma glucose falls, and the counter regulatory response is glucagon release that mobilizes hepatic glycogen. Glucose cannot rise while active insulin is present. Beta cells shut down rather than secrete more when glucose is falling. Injected insulin acts whether or not food is eaten, which is exactly why the timing matters.

cards.q: What is the underlying mechanism of type 1 diabetes mellitus?
cards.a: Autoimmune destruction of the pancreatic beta cells.
options: Failure of the liver to store glycogen
Loss of insulin receptor sensitivity in muscle and fat
Overproduction of glucagon by the alpha cells
Autoimmune destruction of the pancreatic beta cells
cards.explanation: In type 1 the immune system destroys the beta cells, so insulin production is lost almost completely and the person depends on injected insulin. Loss of receptor sensitivity in muscle and fat is the mechanism of type 2. Alpha cell overproduction contributes to the hyperglycemia but is not the primary lesion. Hepatic glycogen storage fails as a consequence of missing insulin rather than as the cause.

cards.q: What is the underlying mechanism of type 2 diabetes mellitus?
cards.a: Target tissues respond poorly to insulin.
options: Target tissues respond poorly to insulin
The beta cells are destroyed by autoantibodies
The pancreas is blocked by a stone in its duct
The kidney fails to reabsorb any filtered glucose
cards.explanation: Type 2 begins with insulin resistance in muscle, liver, and fat, so a normal or even high insulin level cannot keep glucose in range, and over years beta cell output also declines. Autoantibody destruction of beta cells defines type 1. A blocked pancreatic duct affects the exocrine enzymes rather than the islets. Renal reabsorption of glucose is normal in type 2 until the filtered load exceeds the transport maximum.

cards.q: Which type of diabetes mellitus characteristically presents with ketoacidosis?
cards.a: Type 1, because insulin is essentially absent.
options: Type 2, because insulin resistance is severe
Type 1, because insulin is essentially absent
Both types equally, since glucose is high in each
Neither, since ketones come only from a high fat diet
cards.explanation: Ketoacidosis requires almost no insulin, because even a small amount of insulin restrains lipolysis, and that is the situation in type 1 where beta cells have been destroyed. Type 2 patients usually retain enough insulin to keep fat breakdown in check, so they rarely develop it. High glucose alone does not produce ketones, which is why the two types differ here. Dietary fat is not the source, since the ketones are made in the liver from mobilized fatty acids.

cards.q: What is the term for glucose appearing in the urine?
cards.a: Glucosuria.
options: Polyuria
Ketonuria
Glucosuria
Polydipsia
cards.explanation: Glucosuria means glucose in the urine, which happens once the filtered load exceeds what the tubule can reabsorb. Polyuria means a large urine volume, which is a consequence here rather than the name for the glucose itself. Ketonuria is ketone bodies in the urine. Polydipsia means excessive thirst and drinking.

cards.q: What does the transport maximum for glucose in the kidney describe?
cards.a: The highest rate at which the tubule can reabsorb filtered glucose.
options: The rate at which glucose enters muscle cells through GLUT4 carriers
The plasma glucose level at which insulin secretion peaks
The highest rate at which the liver can release new glucose
The highest rate at which the tubule can reabsorb filtered glucose
cards.explanation: The tubule reabsorbs glucose through a fixed number of sodium coupled carriers, and once every carrier is busy no more can be reclaimed, so the excess stays in the tubular fluid. Insulin secretion is a pancreatic event and is not what the term describes. Hepatic glucose release has its own limits but is unrelated to this renal term. GLUT4 uptake happens at the target tissue, not in the nephron.

cards.q: Where are ketone bodies produced?
cards.a: In the liver, from fatty acids.
options: In the liver, from fatty acids
In skeletal muscle, from amino acids
In the pancreas, from stored insulin
In the kidney, from filtered glucose
cards.explanation: The liver takes up fatty acids released from adipose tissue and converts them into ketone bodies, which other tissues can then burn as fuel. Muscle consumes ketones but does not make them, and amino acids are not the substrate. The pancreas secretes hormones and does not produce ketones. The kidney can use ketones but does not generate them from glucose.

cards.q: Why does an untreated diabetic patient feel constantly thirsty?
cards.a: Water lost in the urine raises plasma osmolarity, which drives thirst.
options: Glucose in the blood binds water and makes the mouth feel very dry
Water lost in the urine raises plasma osmolarity, which drives thirst
Insulin normally suppresses the thirst center in the brain
Ketone bodies stimulate the thirst center in the hypothalamus directly
cards.explanation: Glucose dragging water into the urine depletes body water and concentrates the plasma, and the hypothalamic osmoreceptors respond by generating thirst. Blood glucose does not dry the mouth by binding water in that way. Insulin has no direct role in the thirst center. Ketones cause acidosis and nausea rather than driving thirst.

cards.q: Which type of diabetes is strongly associated with obesity and adult onset?
cards.a: Type 2.
options: Type 1
Both are equally associated with obesity
Type 2
Neither is related to body composition
cards.explanation: Type 2 typically appears in adulthood and excess adipose tissue is a major contributor to the insulin resistance that defines it. Type 1 usually appears in childhood or adolescence and is not driven by body composition. Saying both are equally associated ignores the different mechanisms. Body composition clearly matters for type 2, so calling diabetes unrelated to it is wrong as well.

cards.q: A patient has a plasma glucose of 350 mg/dL. The filtered glucose load now exceeds the tubular transport maximum. What appears in the urine?
cards.a: Glucose, because the carriers are saturated.
options: No glucose, because reabsorption rises with the load
Nothing unusual, because the kidney raises its transport maximum
Protein, because glucose damages the filter acutely
Glucose, because the carriers are saturated
cards.explanation: Reabsorption depends on a fixed number of carriers, so once they are all occupied any additional filtered glucose simply passes on into the urine. Reabsorption cannot keep rising indefinitely, which is what having a maximum means. Acute protein loss is not caused by a single high glucose reading. The transport maximum is set by the number of carriers and does not adjust within hours.

cards.q: Why does the large urine volume of untreated hyperglycemia occur?
cards.a: Unreabsorbed glucose holds water in the tubule, an osmotic diuresis.
options: Unreabsorbed glucose holds water in the tubule, an osmotic diuresis
Antidiuretic hormone secretion is suppressed by the high glucose
Glomerular filtration rate doubles when the plasma glucose is high
Aldosterone secretion falls, so both sodium and water are lost
cards.explanation: Glucose left in the tubular fluid is osmotically active, so water that would normally be reabsorbed stays with it and is excreted, which is what osmotic diuresis means. ADH is actually high here, because the patient is losing water and becoming concentrated. Filtration rate does not double. Aldosterone rises rather than falls as volume is lost.

cards.q: A patient has a high plasma glucose together with a high plasma insulin. Which mechanism does this fit?
cards.a: Insulin resistance with beta cells compensating.
options: Complete destruction of the beta cells
Insulin resistance with beta cells compensating
An insulin secreting tumor of the islets
Excess glucagon with normal insulin sensitivity
cards.explanation: Plenty of insulin alongside a high glucose means the hormone is present but the target tissues are not responding, and the beta cells are working harder to make up for it, which is the type 2 pattern. Beta cell destruction would give high glucose with low insulin. An insulin secreting tumor would drive glucose down, not up. Excess glucagon with normal sensitivity would raise glucose but insulin would not be persistently elevated to this degree.

cards.q: Insulin is completely absent. What happens in adipose tissue?
cards.a: Lipolysis runs unchecked and fatty acids flood the plasma.
options: Triglyceride storage increases because glucose is plentiful
Fat cells take up ketone bodies and store them
Lipolysis runs unchecked and fatty acids flood the plasma
Adipose tissue stops responding to any hormone
cards.explanation: Insulin is the main brake on hormone sensitive lipase, so without it fat breakdown accelerates and the liver receives a large fatty acid load, which is the first step toward ketone production. Storage requires insulin, so it cannot increase when insulin is gone. Fat cells do not store ketone bodies. Adipose tissue still responds to catecholamines and cortisol, and both push toward breakdown here.

cards.q: Ketone bodies accumulate in the plasma. Predict blood pH and the pattern of breathing.
cards.a: pH falls and breathing becomes deep and rapid.
options: pH rises and breathing becomes slow and shallow
pH rises and breathing becomes deep and rapid
pH falls and breathing becomes slow and shallow
pH falls and breathing becomes deep and rapid
cards.explanation: Ketone bodies are acids, so they consume bicarbonate and lower blood pH, and the chemoreceptors respond by driving deep rapid breathing to blow off carbon dioxide and limit the fall. A rising pH would mean an alkalosis, which is not what an acid load produces. Slow shallow breathing would worsen the acidosis instead of compensating for it.

cards.q: C peptide is released along with insulin from the beta cell, so measuring it shows how much insulin the person is making. A patient has an undetectable C peptide. Which type does this fit?
cards.a: Type 1, because the beta cells are gone.
options: Type 1, because the beta cells are gone
Type 2, because the tissues are resistant
Type 2, because the liver clears C peptide faster
Neither, since C peptide is unrelated to insulin production
cards.explanation: C peptide is made only when a beta cell processes proinsulin, so an undetectable level means essentially no endogenous insulin is being produced, which is the type 1 picture. Resistance in type 2 leaves C peptide normal or high, since the cells are still secreting. Hepatic clearance differences do not explain an undetectable value. C peptide is produced in a one to one ratio with insulin, so it is directly informative.

cards.q: An untreated type 1 patient eats normally but loses weight steadily. Why?
cards.a: Without insulin, fuel cannot be stored and fat and protein break down.
options: The high glucose suppresses the appetite so food intake falls
Without insulin, fuel cannot be stored and fat and protein break down
Ketone bodies are burned faster than food can supply the fuel
Water loss in the urine accounts for the entire change in body weight
cards.explanation: Insulin is the storage signal, so without it the body behaves as if it is starving, breaking down fat and muscle protein while glucose spills into the urine unused. Appetite is typically increased rather than suppressed. Ketones are made from the person's own fat, so burning them is part of the loss rather than a separate cause. Water loss contributes early but cannot explain steady loss of tissue over weeks.

cards.q: Trace the sequence from absent insulin to the large urine volume of untreated diabetes.
cards.a: Glucose rises, the filtered load exceeds the transport maximum, leftover glucose holds water, and urine volume rises.
options: Glucose rises, antidiuretic hormone is suppressed, the collecting duct loses its aquaporins, and urine volume rises
Glucose rises, plasma osmolarity falls, thirst increases, and urine volume rises along with the extra intake
Glucose rises, the filtered load exceeds the transport maximum, leftover glucose holds water, and urine volume rises
Glucose rises, renal blood flow falls, glomerular filtration rises, and urine volume rises along with it
cards.explanation: The chain is mechanical and osmotic: too much glucose is filtered for the carriers to handle, the leftover glucose keeps water in the tubule, and that water leaves as urine. ADH is high in this patient rather than suppressed, since body water is being lost. Plasma osmolarity rises rather than falls, which is what drives the thirst. Falling renal blood flow would reduce filtration, not increase it.

cards.q: Trace the sequence from absent insulin to a fall in blood pH in a type 1 patient.
cards.a: Lipolysis rises, fatty acids reach the liver, ketone bodies form, and these acids lower pH.
options: Glucose rises, lactic acid is produced by working muscle, and the accumulating acid lowers pH
Water loss concentrates the plasma, which lowers pH by diluting the bicarbonate
Protein breakdown releases ammonia, which lowers pH directly in the blood
Lipolysis rises, fatty acids reach the liver, ketone bodies form, and these acids lower pH
cards.explanation: With insulin gone the brake on fat breakdown is released, the liver converts the incoming fatty acids into acetoacetate and beta hydroxybutyrate, and these acids titrate bicarbonate so pH falls. Lactic acid comes from anaerobic muscle work rather than from a lack of insulin. Ammonia from protein breakdown is converted to urea and does not acidify the blood this way. Concentrating the plasma raises rather than lowers the bicarbonate concentration.

cards.q: Why does a person with type 2 diabetes rarely develop ketoacidosis even with a plasma glucose over 300 mg/dL?
cards.a: Residual insulin is still enough to restrain lipolysis.
options: Residual insulin is still enough to restrain lipolysis
The liver in type 2 has lost the ability to make ketone bodies
Glucagon secretion is absent in type 2 diabetes
The kidney excretes ketone bodies faster in type 2
cards.explanation: It takes very little insulin to hold hormone sensitive lipase in check, and type 2 patients usually still secrete some, so the massive fatty acid delivery that ketoacidosis requires never happens even when glucose is very high. The liver retains its ketogenic capacity in type 2. Glucagon is present and often elevated in type 2. Renal excretion of ketones is not accelerated enough to prevent an acidosis if one were being generated.

cards.q: A person with type 2 diabetes has had a rising plasma glucose over ten years while their measured insulin first rose and then fell. What does this pattern show?
cards.a: Resistance came first, beta cells compensated, then their output declined.
options: The person actually had type 1 diabetes right from the beginning
Resistance came first, beta cells compensated, then their output declined
Insulin was being destroyed by antibodies in the later years of the illness
The liver stopped responding to glucagon over that same time period
cards.explanation: The early rise in insulin is the beta cell response to resistant tissues, and the later fall reflects beta cell function wearing down so glucose climbs further, which is the usual natural history of type 2. Type 1 would show low insulin from the start rather than an initial rise. Antibodies against insulin are not the usual cause of this pattern. Losing hepatic glucagon responsiveness would tend to lower glucose, not raise it.

cards.q: How much glucose does an adult drink for a standard oral glucose tolerance test?
cards.a: 75 grams.
options: 75 grams
50 grams
25 grams
150 grams
cards.explanation: The standard adult load is 75 grams of glucose in solution, a dose large enough to challenge the system in everyone yet standardized so curves can be compared. Twenty five grams is too small to reveal a mild defect. Fifty grams is used in some screening protocols but is not the standard test. One hundred fifty grams is not a routine load.

cards.q: How long should a subject fast before a glucose tolerance test?
cards.a: About 8 to 12 hours.
options: About 2 hours
About 8 to 12 hours
About 24 hours
No fast is needed
cards.explanation: An overnight fast of roughly 8 to 12 hours empties the gut and lets plasma glucose settle to a true baseline without pushing the subject into starvation metabolism. Two hours leaves the previous meal still being absorbed. Twenty four hours shifts the body into fat mobilization and distorts the result. Skipping the fast makes the baseline meaningless.

cards.q: What is a normal fasting plasma glucose?
cards.a: Below 100 mg/dL.
options: Below 200 mg/dL
Below 140 mg/dL
Below 100 mg/dL
Below 60 mg/dL
cards.explanation: A fasting plasma glucose under 100 mg/dL is the normal range and reflects a liver releasing glucose at a rate matched to tissue use. Under 140 mg/dL is the criterion for the two hour sample, not the fasting one. Under 200 mg/dL is far too permissive for a fasting value. Under 60 mg/dL would be hypoglycemia rather than a normal baseline.

cards.q: Which sample is the key one for interpreting a glucose tolerance test?
cards.a: The 2 hour sample.
options: The 30 minute sample
The 1 hour sample
The 4 hour sample
The 2 hour sample
cards.explanation: By two hours a normal subject has cleared the load and returned near baseline, so this time point separates adequate from inadequate handling better than any other. The 30 minute value mostly reflects how fast the drink was absorbed. The 1 hour value is useful for describing the peak but varies widely in healthy people. Four hours is too late, and by then a reactive dip may confuse the reading.

cards.q: What is the normal 2 hour plasma glucose in a glucose tolerance test?
cards.a: Below 140 mg/dL.
options: Below 140 mg/dL
Below 100 mg/dL
Below 200 mg/dL
Below 250 mg/dL
cards.explanation: A two hour value under 140 mg/dL means the insulin response cleared the load on schedule, which is the normal result. Under 100 mg/dL is the fasting criterion and is stricter than the two hour test requires. Under 200 mg/dL includes the impaired range, so it is too loose. Under 250 mg/dL would call clearly abnormal curves normal.

cards.q: Which 2 hour plasma glucose range is called impaired glucose tolerance?
cards.a: 140 to 199 mg/dL.
options: 100 to 125 mg/dL
140 to 199 mg/dL
200 to 250 mg/dL
126 to 139 mg/dL
cards.explanation: A two hour value between 140 and 199 mg/dL is higher than normal but below the diabetic cutoff, so it is labeled impaired glucose tolerance. The 100 to 125 range describes an impaired fasting glucose, a different measurement. Two hundred and above is the diabetic range rather than the impaired one. The 126 to 139 range mixes a fasting cutoff with a two hour band.

cards.q: When plotting a glucose tolerance curve, what belongs on each axis?
cards.a: Time on the x axis and plasma glucose on the y axis.
options: Plasma glucose on the x axis and time on the y axis
Time on the x axis and plasma insulin on the y axis
Time on the x axis and plasma glucose on the y axis
Glucose dose on the x axis and time on the y axis
cards.explanation: Time is the independent variable, since the experimenter chooses when to sample, so it goes on the x axis while the measured glucose goes on the y axis. Reversing them would put the measured value on the axis reserved for the variable under control. Plasma insulin is a different measurement and is not the curve being asked for. The glucose dose is a single fixed value and is not plotted at all.

cards.q: In a normal subject, when does plasma glucose reach its peak after the drink?
cards.a: Between 30 and 60 minutes.
options: Within about 5 minutes
At about 3 hours after the drink
At about 2 hours after the drink
Between 30 and 60 minutes
cards.explanation: Absorption from the gut takes time, so the peak arrives about half an hour to an hour after the drink and then insulin brings it down. Five minutes is too soon for a meaningful amount to be absorbed. At two hours a normal subject is already back near baseline. Three hours may show a slight dip below baseline rather than a peak.

cards.q: A subject has a fasting glucose of 92 mg/dL, a 1 hour value of 155 mg/dL, and a 2 hour value of 120 mg/dL. How do you classify this curve?
cards.a: Normal.
options: Normal
Impaired glucose tolerance
Diabetic range
Uninterpretable without an insulin measurement
cards.explanation: The fasting value is under 100 mg/dL and the two hour value is under 140 mg/dL, so both criteria are met and the peak at one hour is expected. Impaired tolerance would need a two hour value of 140 or more. The diabetic range starts at 200 mg/dL at two hours. Insulin measurements add information but are not needed to classify the glucose curve.

cards.q: A subject has a fasting glucose of 108 mg/dL and a 2 hour value of 165 mg/dL. How do you classify this curve?
cards.a: Impaired glucose tolerance.
options: A normal curve
Impaired glucose tolerance
The diabetic range
A hypoglycemic pattern
cards.explanation: A two hour value of 165 mg/dL sits in the 140 to 199 band, which is above normal but below the diabetic cutoff, so this curve is impaired. Normal would require the two hour value to be under 140 mg/dL. The diabetic range begins at 200 mg/dL at two hours. A hypoglycemic pattern would dip below the fasting level, not stay above it.

cards.q: A subject has a fasting glucose of 140 mg/dL and a 2 hour value of 245 mg/dL. Where does this curve fall?
cards.a: In the diabetic range at both time points.
options: In the normal range at both time points
In the impaired range at both time points
In the diabetic range at both time points
In the impaired range fasting and the normal range at 2 hours
cards.explanation: A fasting value of 140 mg/dL is above the 126 mg/dL cutoff and a two hour value of 245 mg/dL is above 200 mg/dL, so both readings fall in the diabetic range. Neither value is anywhere near normal. The impaired bands stop at 125 mg/dL fasting and 199 mg/dL at two hours. The two hour value cannot be normal when it is well above 140 mg/dL.

cards.q: One curve peaks higher than normal and returns to baseline much more slowly. What does the slow return say about insulin?
cards.a: Insulin action is inadequate for the load.
options: Insulin is being cleared from plasma too slowly
Insulin is being secreted too early
Insulin is acting normally but absorption was slow
Insulin action is inadequate for the load
cards.explanation: The rate at which glucose comes back down reflects how effectively insulin moves it into tissue and shuts off hepatic output, so a slow return means the insulin response is too small, too late, or blunted by resistance. Early secretion would speed the return, not slow it. Slow absorption would flatten the peak instead of raising it. Slow insulin clearance would leave more insulin around and hasten the fall.

cards.q: Which feature of a glucose tolerance curve most directly reflects how well the tissues respond to insulin?
cards.a: How quickly glucose returns toward the fasting level.
options: How quickly glucose returns toward the fasting level
The height of the fasting value at time zero
The time at which the glucose drink was given
The total volume of the glucose solution swallowed
cards.explanation: Clearance of the load is the functional test, so the downslope from peak back to baseline is where insulin sensitivity and secretion show themselves. The fasting value is informative about baseline hepatic output but not about the response to a challenge. The time the drink was given only sets the zero point on the axis. The volume of solution is standardized and does not vary with the subject.

cards.q: A subject ate breakfast an hour before arriving for the test. How does this affect the fasting sample?
cards.a: The baseline is falsely high, so the whole curve is shifted.
options: The baseline is falsely low, so the peak looks larger
The baseline is falsely high, so the whole curve is shifted
The baseline is unaffected, since the meal was small
The baseline is unaffected, but the 2 hour value is falsely low
cards.explanation: Absorbed carbohydrate from breakfast is still raising plasma glucose, so the sample labeled fasting is not a true baseline and every later value is being compared against the wrong starting point. Eating raises the baseline rather than lowering it. Even a small meal moves plasma glucose within an hour. The two hour value would tend to be falsely high, not low, since the subject started higher.

cards.q: A technician plots points at 0, 30, 60, 90, and 120 minutes. What units belong on the two axes?
cards.a: Minutes on the x axis and mg/dL on the y axis.
options: Minutes on the x axis and grams on the y axis
mg/dL on the x axis and minutes on the y axis
Minutes on the x axis and mg/dL on the y axis
Hours on the x axis and mOsm/L on the y axis
cards.explanation: The sampling times are in minutes and the measured quantity is a plasma glucose concentration in mg/dL, so those are the units on x and y. Reversing them puts the measurement on the time axis. Grams describe the dose swallowed, not the plasma concentration. Osmolarity in mOsm/L is a different measurement entirely.

cards.q: Two subjects both peak at 180 mg/dL. Subject A is back to 105 mg/dL at 2 hours and subject B is at 170 mg/dL. What does the difference tell you?
cards.a: Subject B clears glucose poorly, so the insulin response is inadequate.
options: Subject A absorbed the glucose drink more slowly than subject B
Subject A has a smaller total body water volume than subject B
Subject B has a higher glomerular filtration rate than subject A
Subject B clears glucose poorly, so the insulin response is inadequate
cards.explanation: An identical peak means both absorbed a similar amount at a similar rate, so the difference lies entirely in the downslope, which is the part of the curve that depends on insulin doing its job. Slower absorption in subject A would have lowered the peak rather than leaving it equal. Filtration rate does not clear glucose at these plasma levels, since it is reabsorbed. Body water differences would change the peak height, not the rate of return.

cards.q: A subject's curve peaks at 165 mg/dL at 45 minutes, returns to 95 mg/dL at 2 hours, then falls to 62 mg/dL at 3 hours with sweating and shakiness. What is the best interpretation?
cards.a: The insulin response was excessive or too prolonged for the load.
options: The insulin response was excessive or too prolonged for the load
The subject failed to absorb the glucose drink
The kidney excreted the excess glucose after 2 hours
The liver stopped releasing glucose because glucagon was absent from birth
cards.explanation: The load was handled well through two hours, so the dip below baseline afterward points to insulin still acting after the glucose supply is exhausted, which produces the sympathetic symptoms of a low glucose. Poor absorption would have prevented the normal peak at 45 minutes. Renal excretion does not occur at these plasma levels, which are well under the transport maximum. A lifelong absence of glucagon would have shown itself long before this test.

cards.q: A subject has a normal fasting glucose of 96 mg/dL but a 2 hour value of 180 mg/dL. What does this combination suggest?
cards.a: Fasting control is intact but the load response is impaired.
options: Both the fasting and the post load values are normal
Fasting control is intact but the load response is impaired
Fasting control has failed while the load response is normal
The samples must have been switched, since this cannot occur
cards.explanation: A normal fasting value shows that basal hepatic output and basal insulin are in balance, while the high two hour value shows the extra insulin needed for a large load is inadequate, which is why the tolerance test finds problems a fasting sample misses. Calling both normal ignores a two hour value above 140 mg/dL. Fasting control has not failed, since 96 mg/dL is normal. This is a common pattern rather than an impossible one.

cards.q: You are given these values: 0 min 118 mg/dL, 60 min 240 mg/dL, 120 min 210 mg/dL. Calculate the change from fasting to 2 hours and classify the curve.
cards.a: A rise of 92 mg/dL, and the 2 hour value is in the diabetic range.
options: A rise of 122 mg/dL, and the 2 hour value is in the impaired range
A rise of 92 mg/dL, and the 2 hour value is in the impaired range
A rise of 92 mg/dL, and the 2 hour value is in the diabetic range
A fall of 30 mg/dL, and the curve is normal
cards.explanation: Two hundred ten minus one hundred eighteen is ninety two, and a two hour value of 210 mg/dL sits above the 200 mg/dL cutoff, so this curve is in the diabetic range. The impaired band stops at 199 mg/dL, so 210 does not qualify. A rise of 122 would be the change from fasting to the 60 minute peak, not to two hours. The fall of 30 mg/dL is the drop from peak to two hours and does not describe the change from fasting.

cards.q: What is a standard curve in a hormone immunoassay?
cards.a: A plot of signal against known hormone concentrations.
options: A plot of the unknown samples in order of measurement
A plot of signal against known hormone concentrations
A record of how the signal drifts over time in one well
A plot of antibody concentration against incubation time
cards.explanation: Samples of known concentration are run alongside the unknowns and their readings define the relationship between signal and concentration, which is what lets an unknown reading be converted into a number. Plotting the unknowns in order tells you nothing about concentration. Signal drift in a single well is a quality problem rather than a calibration. Antibody concentration is held constant across the plate.

cards.q: What molecule gives an immunoassay its specificity for one hormone?
cards.a: An antibody raised against that hormone.
options: A dye that binds only that hormone
An enzyme that cleaves only that hormone
An antibody raised against that hormone
A membrane pore sized to that hormone
cards.explanation: The assay works because an antibody binds one target with high selectivity, so it can pick that hormone out of a plasma sample containing thousands of other proteins. A dye binds by chemical class rather than by molecular identity. An enzyme that cleaves the hormone would destroy the thing being measured. Pore size separates by size alone and cannot distinguish two similar molecules.

cards.q: In a standard ELISA, what does the enzyme attached to the detection antibody actually produce?
cards.a: A colored product whose intensity is measured.
options: Heat that is measured by a thermometer
More of the hormone being measured
A precipitate that removes the hormone from solution
A colored product whose intensity is measured
cards.explanation: The enzyme converts a colorless substrate into a colored product, and because each bound enzyme keeps working, the color builds in proportion to how much hormone was captured. The enzyme does not make more hormone, which would defeat the measurement. A precipitate is not how a plate reader quantifies the result. Heat output is far too small to serve as the signal.

cards.q: Which instrument reads the result of a colorimetric ELISA?
cards.a: A spectrophotometer or plate reader.
options: A spectrophotometer or plate reader
A refrigerated benchtop centrifuge
A pH meter with a glass electrode
An electrophoresis chamber and power supply
cards.explanation: A plate reader is a spectrophotometer that passes light of a chosen wavelength through each well and reports absorbance, which is the signal the standard curve is built from. A centrifuge separates by density and does not measure color. A pH meter reports hydrogen ion activity. An electrophoresis chamber separates molecules by charge and size.

cards.q: In an assay run, what is the unknown?
cards.a: The sample whose hormone concentration is being determined.
options: The antibody used to capture the hormone in the well
The sample whose hormone concentration is being determined
The wavelength that the plate reader has been set to
The substrate added to each well to develop the color signal
cards.explanation: The unknown is the patient or experimental sample, and the entire point of running standards alongside it is to convert its signal into a concentration. The capture antibody is a known reagent chosen in advance. The reading wavelength is set by the operator. The substrate is a known reagent added in equal amounts to every well.

cards.q: How many antibodies bind the hormone in a sandwich ELISA?
cards.a: Two, a capture antibody and a detection antibody.
options: One, which both captures and reports
Three, one for each region of the hormone
Two, a capture antibody and a detection antibody
None, since the hormone binds the plate directly
cards.explanation: One antibody fixed to the well captures the hormone and a second labeled antibody binds a different site on it, so the hormone is sandwiched between them and only the captured molecules generate signal. A single antibody cannot both anchor and report in this format. Three antibodies are not part of the standard design. Direct binding to the plate would lose the specificity the capture antibody provides.

cards.q: What is the purpose of a blank well in an assay?
cards.a: To measure background signal with no hormone present.
options: To provide extra sample in case a well is spilled
To hold the highest standard for comparison
To check that the plate reader lamp is warm
To measure background signal with no hormone present
cards.explanation: The blank contains everything except the hormone, so its reading is the signal produced by reagents alone and it is subtracted from the others to leave the true hormone dependent signal. The highest standard is a separate well with a known high concentration. Lamp warm up is handled by the instrument itself. A spare volume of sample is not what a blank is for.

cards.q: On a standard curve, which axis holds concentration?
cards.a: The x axis.
options: The x axis
The y axis
Either one, since the plot is symmetric
Neither, since concentration is not plotted
cards.explanation: Concentration is the variable the experimenter sets in the standards, so it goes on the x axis while the measured absorbance goes on the y axis. Putting concentration on the y axis reverses the roles of the known and the measured variable. The plot is not symmetric, since one variable is controlled and the other is observed. Concentration must be plotted or the curve could not be used.

cards.q: Standards read 0.40 absorbance at 10 ng/mL and 0.80 at 20 ng/mL. An unknown reads 0.60. What is its approximate concentration?
cards.a: About 15 ng/mL.
options: About 5 ng/mL
About 15 ng/mL
About 12 ng/mL
About 30 ng/mL
cards.explanation: An absorbance of 0.60 lies exactly halfway between the two standards, so on a linear portion of the curve the concentration is halfway between 10 and 20 ng/mL. Five is below the lower standard and would give a much smaller reading. Twelve does not sit at the midpoint of the bracket. Thirty is above the higher standard and would give a reading above 0.80.

cards.q: An unknown reads an absorbance higher than the highest standard. What should be done?
cards.a: Dilute the sample and run it again.
options: Report it as equal to the highest standard
Extend the straight line beyond the last point and read off a value
Dilute the sample and run it again
Report it as unmeasurable and discard the sample
cards.explanation: Above the top standard the curve is no longer defined, so the sample must be diluted into the working range and the result multiplied back by the dilution factor. Reporting it as equal to the top standard understates the true value. Extending the line assumes linearity where the assay is usually flattening out. Discarding the sample throws away a result that a simple dilution can recover.

cards.q: In a competitive immunoassay, labeled hormone and sample hormone compete for a limited number of antibody sites. What is the relationship between signal and concentration?
cards.a: Signal falls as sample concentration rises.
options: Signal rises as sample concentration rises
Signal rises and then falls as concentration rises
Signal is independent of sample concentration
Signal falls as sample concentration rises
cards.explanation: More unlabeled hormone in the sample displaces labeled hormone from the antibody, so less label stays bound and the measured signal goes down, which makes the curve run downhill. A rising signal is the pattern of a sandwich assay, where the hormone is captured rather than displaced. Independence would mean the assay measures nothing. A rise then fall does not describe simple competition for binding sites.

cards.q: A technician skips the wash steps before adding substrate. What happens to the readings?
cards.a: All wells read too high, because unbound label was not removed.
options: All wells read too high, because unbound label was not removed
All wells read too low, because the antibody was diluted
Only the blank reads too high, since it has no hormone
Only the highest standard is affected, because it saturates
cards.explanation: Washing removes labeled antibody that never bound the target, so skipping it leaves that label in every well and every reading is inflated by background. The antibody is not diluted by omitting a wash, so a low reading is not expected. The problem affects the whole plate rather than the blank alone. Saturation is a separate issue and does not confine the error to one well.

cards.q: A plasma sample is diluted 1 in 10, and the diluted sample reads 5 ng/mL from the standard curve. What was the concentration in the original plasma?
cards.a: 50 ng/mL.
options: 0.5 ng/mL
50 ng/mL
5 ng/mL
500 ng/mL
cards.explanation: A one in ten dilution reduces the concentration tenfold, so the original must be ten times the measured value, or 50 ng/mL. Half a nanogram per milliliter would come from multiplying in the wrong direction twice. Five is the diluted reading and ignores the dilution entirely. Five hundred applies a hundredfold correction that was not performed.

cards.q: Why are standards run on the same plate as the unknowns rather than on a plate from last week?
cards.a: Because reagent activity and conditions vary between runs.
options: Because the hormone changes structure over a week
Because the plate reader can only store one curve
Because reagent activity and conditions vary between runs
Because antibodies bind more tightly on a fresh plate every time
cards.explanation: Enzyme activity, incubation temperature, and development time all differ from run to run, so a curve built under this run's conditions is the only valid reference for this run's unknowns. The hormone in a properly stored standard does not change structure that fast. Instrument storage capacity is not the reason. Binding affinity is a property of the antibody rather than of plate freshness.

cards.q: A standard curve is linear from 0 to 20 ng/mL and then flattens. An unknown reads an absorbance that falls on the flat part. Why is the reported value unreliable?
cards.a: On the flat part a large change in concentration barely changes the signal.
options: On the flat part the enzyme has been washed out of the wells
On the flat part the antibody has stopped binding the hormone entirely
On the flat part the reading is always exactly double the true value
On the flat part a large change in concentration barely changes the signal
cards.explanation: Where the curve plateaus the binding sites are nearly all occupied, so a wide range of concentrations produce almost the same absorbance and a small reading error translates into a huge concentration error. The antibody has not stopped binding, it is simply saturated. There is no fixed factor of two relating reading to truth. The enzyme is still present, since it is what generates the plateau signal.

cards.q: Two replicate wells of the same unknown read 0.42 and 0.78 absorbance. What is the best conclusion?
cards.a: Something went wrong in the wells, so the sample should be run again.
options: Something went wrong in the wells, so the sample should be run again
Take the average, since replicates are meant to be averaged
Take the higher value, since loss of signal is the common error
Take the lower value, since background always inflates readings
cards.explanation: Replicates that differ by nearly a factor of two point to a pipetting or washing error rather than ordinary scatter, so averaging two numbers when one is wrong just splits the difference between a good value and a bad one. Averaging is appropriate only when replicates agree closely. Choosing the higher or lower value assumes you know which error occurred, and here you do not.

cards.q: A control sample known to contain 20 ng/mL reads 30 ng/mL on this run. What does that tell you about the other results on the plate?
cards.a: They are probably all overestimated, so the run should be repeated.
options: Only the control well is affected, so the other results stand
They are probably all overestimated, so the run should be repeated
The standard curve is fine, since controls are not part of it
The unknowns are underestimated by the same proportion
cards.explanation: A control exists to test whether the whole plate is reading truly, so a control that comes out fifty percent high signals a systematic problem that would affect every well processed alongside it. Treating the control as an isolated well defeats the purpose of running one. The standard curve is exactly what a bad control calls into question. An overreading control implies overestimation of the unknowns, not underestimation.

cards.q: Standards read 0.20 at 5 ng/mL, 0.40 at 10 ng/mL, and 0.60 at 15 ng/mL. An unknown reads 0.50. What is its concentration, and what makes this calculation valid?
cards.a: About 12.5 ng/mL, because the standards fall on a straight line.
options: About 10 ng/mL, because that is the middle standard
About 25 ng/mL, because absorbance and concentration are inverse
About 12.5 ng/mL, because the standards fall on a straight line
About 12.5 ng/mL, but only if the assay is competitive
cards.explanation: Absorbance rises by 0.20 for every 5 ng/mL, so the relationship is linear across this range and a reading of 0.50 sits midway between the 10 and 15 ng/mL standards. Ten would be the answer only if the reading matched the middle standard, which it does not. An inverse relationship would show absorbance falling as concentration rose, which these standards contradict. A competitive assay would give a downward sloping curve, so it is not what these numbers describe.
